articles.title: El-Sayed on Piker: Not interested ‘in having a conversation about streamers in California’
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday pushed back on questions about far-left streamer Hasan Piker, who he previously campaigned with. “There are Jewish voters in your state who are concerned about your relationship with Piker. You have condemned antisemitism but not called out his rhetoric directly. Why not?” CBS News’s Weijia Jiang asked…
articles.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday pushed back on questions about far-left streamer Hasan Piker, who he previously campaigned with.

“There are Jewish voters in your state who are concerned about your relationship with Piker. You have condemned antisemitism but not called out his rhetoric directly. Why not?” CBS News’s Weijia Jiang asked El-Sayed on “Face the Nation.”

“Weiija, with all due respect, this is the third time you’ve asked about a Twitch streamer in California. I’ve done four events in Michigan this week. You know what didn’t come up? Twitch streamers in California,” El-Sayed responded.

“You know what did come up? Grocery prices, the fact that people can’t see a doctor, the worry that they have about the quality of air and water. I’m not interested in having a conversation about streamers in California because they are not raising the prices of gas and groceries,” he added.

The Michigan Senate candidate is one of multiple insurgent progressive Democratic candidates who were able to lock down a spot in the general election in primaries this summer. He has received backing from fellow left-wing figures like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.)

El-Sayed has also campaigned with Piker, a left-wing streamer with a history of controversial comments.

Late last month , El-Sayed said he had “no plans” to campaign with Piker in the wake of multiple Democratic lawmakers criticizing the streamer over his comments on American Jews supporting Israel.

Piker, a heavy critic of Israel and its actions in Gaza, recently said that while Jewish Americans do not automatically back the government of Israel, “Jewish institutions” are “teaching people the idea that Jews are monolithic.”

“If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews,” Piker said on a livestream.

articles.title: Poll: Democratic voters driven by Trump opposition more than party platform
articles.summary: A new poll shows that Democratic voters are more driven to cast their ballots in the November midterms elections out of their opposition to President Trump more so than the party’s platform. The CBS News/YouGov poll released Sunday found that 54 percent of Democratic voters said they will vote for their Democratic candidate to Congress…
articles.body:
A new poll shows that Democratic voters are more driven to cast their ballots in the November midterms elections out of their opposition to President Trump more so than the party’s platform.

The CBS News/YouGov poll released Sunday found that 54 percent of Democratic voters said they will vote for their Democratic candidate to Congress to stop Trump and Republican lawmakers from passing their policies, and 46 percent said they will vote Democratic to help the party pass its policies.

More Republican voters said they intend to vote to help Trump and Republicans pass their policies at 57 percent, while 43 percent said they will vote to stop Democrats from having their policies passed.

Forty-five percent of voters in general told pollsters that they will vote to oppose Trump, with 28 percent saying they will vote in support of him and 27 percent saying their vote isn’t about Trump.

Other questions to registered voters were split. As to whether Democratic policies will improve voters’ finances if they take control of Congress, 36 percent each said they would be financially better off or worse off. The question of whether Democratic policies will help protect or threaten “your culture and way of life” received 37 percent for either possibility.

The poll also showed that Trump’s job approval is at 39 percent, with 61 percent who disapprove.

Voters noted that Trump’s endorsement of GOP candidates make them less likely to support a candidate, at 48 percent compared to 21 percent who told pollsters that it would make them more likely to vote in November.

The election handicapper Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, last week shifted the GOP’s odds of winning the Senate to 51 percent, down from the 60 percent chance they had two months ago.

DDHQ’s estimate for the House shows Democrats holding a 68 percent chance of reclaiming the House, with a 32 percent probability for Republicans.

James Blair, a top adviser to Trump, told NBC News’s podcast that the president is “ cautiously optimistic ” that Republicans will maintain their control of Congress, with Trump himself making another pitch for Republicans at the party’s midterm convention in Dallas last week.

Recent polling shows voters have soured on Trump’s job performance, specifically his handling of the economy and the deeply unpopular Iran war.

The CBS News/YouGov survey was conducted Sept. 8-11 and included 2,460 respondents. The margin of error is 2.3 percentage points.

articles.standfirst: Investigação é um desdobramento de operação deflagrada em 2025 para apurar suspeitas de desvio de emendas parlamentares.
articles.summary: Cezinha de Madureira é alvo da Operação Transparência da PF, que investiga tráfico de influência em tribunais.
articles.body:
O deputado federal Cezinha de Madureira (PL-SP) em foto do dia 8 de outubro de 2025 — Foto: Bruno Spada/Câmara dos Deputados

A Polícia Federal (PF) deflagrou, nesta segunda-feira (14), a terceira fase da Operação Transparência, que investiga suspeitas de corrupção, lavagem de dinheiro e tráfico de influência junto a tribunais superiores.

Segundo informações obtidas pela TV Globo, o deputado federal Cezinha de Madureira (PL-SP) está entre os alvos. A reportagem procurou o deputado, mas ainda não obteve resposta.

Policiais federais cumprem quatro mandados de busca e apreensão, expedidos pelo ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) Flávio Dino, no Distrito Federal e em São Paulo.

Segundo as investigações, integrantes do grupo teriam cobrado valores altos em troca da promessa de influenciar decisões judiciais em processos ainda em andamento.

A ação é desdobramento de investigação iniciada em dezembro de 2025, que apura suspeitas de desvio de emendas parlamentares.

🔎O ministro Flávio Dino é responsável por autorizar a operação porque ele é relator de processos na Corte que investigam suspeitas de desvios e falta de transparência ligada à destinação das emendas — recursos públicos enviados por parlamentares a suas bases eleitorais.

articles.title: Ministros do STF discutem se Moraes e Mendonça devem participar de julgamento na terça | G1
articles.standfirst: Quórum da sessão pode ser uma das questões preliminares a serem debatidas. Nos bastidores, ministros não descartam pedido de vista ou até adiamento da sessão para discutir caso de Moraes.
articles.summary: Quórum da sessão pode ser uma das questões preliminares a serem debatidas. Nos bastidores, ministros não descartam pedido de vista ou até adiamento da sessão para discutir caso de Moraes.
articles.body:
O Supremo Tribunal Federal chega às vésperas da sessão desta terça-feira (15) que pode decidir sobre a abertura de uma apuração contra o ministro Alexandre de Moraes por mensagens enviadas por Daniel Vorcaro sem definição do rito e principalmente do quórum que vai analisar o relatório da Polícia Federal.

Ministros discutem nos bastidores se os colegas Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça devem participar da sessão que vai decidir sobre a regularidade do relatório.

Até agora, o Supremo só confirmou que a sessão será transmitida na TV Justiça e o acesso ao plenário restrito.

Alvo do relatório da Polícia Federal que apontou 52 mensagens de Vorcaro , Moraes indicou em conversas internas que ainda não teria decidido se vai ou não pedir para se manifestar e até mesmo votar.

Uma ala do Supremo avalia que o ideal seria que Moraes não comparecesse ao plenário para não representar um movimento de pressão sobre os colegas.

Já ministros alinhados com Moraes também discutem se vão levantar uma questão de ordem para que o ministro André Mendonça não possa participar da análise do caso.

Os ministros Alexandre de Moraes e André Mendonça, do Supremo Tribunal Federal — Foto: REUTERS/Adriano Machado

O argumento é de que os questionamentos pela condução do relatório sobre Moraes impediria que votasse no caso.

A Procuradoria-Geral da República defendeu a nulidade do relatório e argumentou que Mendonça não só direcionou a busca de dados contra Moraes pela PF, como não consultou a Presidência sobre as medidas contra os colegas. Portanto, uma das possibilidades é que, se os ministros não decidirem o afastamento por iniciativa própria, o caso possa ser colocado para discussão do plenário.

Ao assumir a relatoria do caso de Moraes para a sessão, o presidente do STF , Edson Fachin, afirmou que, a depender do resultado da sessão, poderia ser aplicado trecho do Código de Processo Civil sobre o impedimento do relator.

Fachin conversou com Mendonça no sábado (12) sobre a medida, que foi elogiada por ministros alinhados a Moraes.

Fachin rejeita discutir na mesma sessão os casos dos ministros Moraes e Mendonça — Foto: Jornal Nacional/Reprodução

Outra possiblidade é que os ministros ainda discutam a participação de outros ministros que supostamente teriam algum tipo de citação no caso Master, como Dias Toffoli , Kassio Nunes Marques e Luiz Fux .

Toffoli deixou a relatoria do caso Master após a PF apontar relação do ministro e empresa da família com Vorcaro. Em relação a Nunes e Fux há uma possível menção a filhos dos ministros no material. Os três ministros negam qualquer irregularidade. A tendência é que o plenário apoie a participação de Fux e Nunes Marques.

O quórum da sessão pode ser uma das questões preliminares a ser debatida.

Nos bastidores, ministros não descartam um pedido de vista ou até mesmo o adiamento da sessão para discutir caso de Moraes. Outro ponto em aberto é se não haverá discussão sobre a sessão ser fechada.

articles.title: Como funciona a folga eleitoral e quais são seus direitos? | G1
articles.standfirst: Quem trabalha como mesário ou é convocado pela Justiça Eleitoral para outros serviços relacionados às eleições, tem direito a dois dias de compensação por cada dia trabalhado.
articles.summary: Quem trabalha como mesário ou é convocado pela Justiça Eleitoral para outros serviços relacionados às eleições, tem direito a dois dias de compensação por cada dia trabalhado.
articles.body:
Mesário conferindo documento / Eleição — Foto: Tomaz Silva/Agência Brasil

Quem trabalha nas eleições como mesário ou exerce outra função convocada pela Justiça Eleitoral tem direito à chamada "folga eleitoral" . O benefício garante dois dias de folga para cada dia de serviço prestado, sem desconto no salário ou prejuízo de outros direitos trabalhistas .

A regra vale apenas para quem tem vínculo empregatício, seja na iniciativa privada ou no serviço público. O benefício é garantido pela Lei das Eleições (Lei nº 9.504/1997).

Têm direito à folga os eleitores convocados pela Justiça Eleitoral para atuar nas eleições, como:

pessoas requisitadas para auxiliar os trabalhos eleitorais.

Quantos dias de folga o trabalhador recebe?

Para cada dia trabalhado nas eleições, o trabalhador tem direito a dois dias de folga. Na conta entram não apenas os dias de votação, mas também os treinamentos oficiais promovidos pela Justiça Eleitoral.

Por exemplo: se um mesário participar de um dia de treinamento. trabalhar no primeiro turno e trabalhar no segundo turno, terá direito a seis dias de folga (três dias de serviço multiplicados por dois) .

A folga vale para trabalhadores da iniciativa privada?

Sim. O direito vale para trabalhadores com carteira assinada (CLT) e também para servidores públicos , desde que tenham vínculo de trabalho no período em que foram convocados pela Justiça Eleitoral.

As folgas devem ser concedidas sem desconto no salário, nas férias ou em qualquer outra vantagem trabalhista .

Os dias de folga devem ser definidos em comum acordo entre o trabalhador e o empregador. As dispensas podem ser concedidas de uma só vez ou em datas diferentes, desde que seja respeitado o direito do trabalhador e considerada a organização da empresa ou do órgão público.

Para solicitar a folga, o trabalhador deve apresentar a declaração de participação fornecida pela Justiça Eleitoral. O documento informa os dias em que o eleitor prestou serviço e serve como comprovação para a concessão das folgas.

O direito à folga está vinculado ao emprego existente no momento da convocação para o serviço eleitoral. Caso haja mudança de emprego ou interrupção do vínculo de trabalho, a utilização das folgas deverá ser ajustada conforme a situação, para garantir o exercício do benefício.

Há outros benefícios para quem trabalha nas eleições?

Sim. Além das folgas compensatórias, quem atua como mesário ou auxiliar da Justiça Eleitoral também pode receber outros benefícios, que não são concedidos pela empresa empregadora, como:

auxílio-alimentação nos dias de votação;

vantagem como critério de desempate em concursos públicos, quando previsto no edital;

aproveitamento da atividade como horas complementares em instituições de ensino que adotem essa possibilidade.

articles.title: Veja entrevista de Frederico Antunes (PSD) à RBS TV | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato do PSD ao Senado participou da primeira entrevista ao vivo da série do Bom Dia Rio Grande nesta segunda-feira (14).
articles.summary: Candidato do PSD ao Senado participou da primeira entrevista ao vivo da série do Bom Dia Rio Grande nesta segunda-feira (14).
articles.body:
O candidato do PSD ao Senado pelo Rio Grande do Sul, Frederico Antunes, foi entrevistado nesta segunda-feira (14) pelo Bom Dia Rio Grande, da RBS TV.

Na entrevista, que durou 15 minutos, Antunes defendeu a prorrogação da suspensão do pagamento das parcelas da dívida do estado com a União .

Segundo Antunes, a negociação será um dos desafios do início de 2027. O candidato afirmou que os recursos devem permanecer no Rio Grande do Sul para financiar a recuperação dos prejuízos provocados pelos eventos climáticos de 2024 e preparar o estado para novas enchentes e estiagens.

"Nós temos um desafio já no início de 2027, primeiro trimestre de 2027, de conseguirmos fazer a prorrogação deste prazo de não pagamento das mensalidades da dívida", afirmou.

Antunes também falou sobre a revisão da escala de trabalho 6x1 , obras de prevenção a eventos climáticos , o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) , fundos constitucionais , financiamento da saúde e dívidas dos produtores rurais .

Frederico Cantori Antunes tem 57 anos, é natural de Uruguaiana e engenheiro agrônomo. Em 1992, estreou na política ao ser eleito vereador de Uruguaiana, aos 24 anos. Em 1998, foi eleito deputado estadual. Depois, foi reeleito para outros seis mandatos consecutivos. Presidiu a Assembleia Legislativa em 2007 e foi líder do governo Eduardo Leite (PSD) na Assembleia em 2019.

A entrevista abriu a série do Bom Dia Rio Grande com os candidatos ao Senado nas eleições de 2026. Os candidatos de partidos, coligações e federações que possuem pelo menos cinco representantes no Congresso Nacional participam ao vivo. Os demais são entrevistados em reportagens gravadas.

A ordem foi definida em sorteio na presença dos representantes dos candidatos. As entrevistas ao vivo têm duração de 15 minutos. Veja o calendário:

14 de setembro: Frederico Antunes (PSD), ao vivo;

15 de setembro: Sanderson (PL), ao vivo;

16 de setembro: Milton Cardoso (PSDB), ao vivo;

17 de setembro: entrevistas gravadas com Ric Jones (PCO), Regis Ethur (PSTU), Luciano do MLB (UP) e Daniela Maidana da Silva (PSTU);

18 de setembro: Manuela D'Avila (PSOL), ao vivo;

21 de setembro: Paulo Pimenta (PT), ao vivo;

22 de setembro: Renato Jaguarão (Cidadania), ao vivo;

23 de setembro: Germano Rigotto (MDB), ao vivo;

24 de setembro: Marcel Van Hattem (NOVO), ao vivo.

Antunes afirmou que pretende atuar no Senado para prorrogar o período em que o estado não precisa pagar as parcelas da dívida com a União . Segundo o candidato, os recursos devem ser usados em investimentos considerados essenciais para a recuperação dos danos provocados pelos eventos climáticos de 2024 e para ampliar a capacidade de prevenção do estado.

Antunes também defendeu que a União considere o impacto de enchentes e estiagens sobre a economia gaúcha. Ele afirmou que as perdas na produção agrícola provocam redução do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) e da arrecadação estadual.

"A nossa economia tem um lastro muito forte do setor primário, do setor da produção agrícola, pecuário. E cada vez que nós temos estiagens, não é só enchente, nós tivemos estiagens no estado do Rio Grande do Sul, nós temos a diminuição brusca da nossa economia", disse.

Questionado sobre críticas à velocidade dos investimentos em prevenção a eventos climáticos, Antunes afirmou que obras de grande porte dependem da elaboração de projetos, de licenciamentos e de um período prolongado de execução. O candidato mencionou a necessidade de construir e reforçar diques.

"Como é que tu vai fazer uma obra dessa em pouco espaço de tempo? Não há condições de fazer isso", afirmou. "Nós recém começamos a trabalhar projetos, ou seja, muitos já estão sendo vistos. Outros precisam ser colocados em prática", disse.

O candidato voltou a relacionar a prevenção a eventos climáticos à negociação da dívida. Para ele, a manutenção dos recursos no estado permitiria a continuidade das obras.

Antunes afirmou ser favorável à revisão da escala de trabalho 6x1. Segundo o candidato, no entanto, a regulamentação deve considerar as características de cada atividade. Ele citou hospitais, Santas Casas e instituições filantrópicas como exemplos de serviços que precisam funcionar durante 24 horas e não poderiam ser tratados da mesma forma que atividades administrativas.

"Não é só dizer que ele vai ter mais tempo para descanso, ele tem que ter também emprego, ele tem que ter trabalho, ele tem que ter renda", disse. "Tu tens que ter o cuidado e a cautela da implantação, inclusive criar um tempo para a implantação desta mudança que se pretende ter", afirmou.

Questionado sobre possíveis mudanças relacionadas ao Supremo Tribunal Federal, incluindo o processo de indicação de ministros, o candidato afirmou que as leis devem ser cumpridas por todos e que o Senado deve cobrar das instituições o cumprimento das respectivas atribuições.

"Lei tem que ser cumprida, tanto para quem usa chinelo quanto para quem usa toga. Tu não pode ter castas com privilégios", disse. "A responsabilidade de estar no Senado da República é a responsabilidade de cobrar das instituições que elas cumpram o seu papel", afirmou.

O candidato defendeu que o Rio Grande do Sul tenha acesso a recursos semelhantes aos disponibilizados pelos fundos constitucionais das regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste.

Segundo Antunes, esses fundos oferecem recursos com custos menores para investimentos e geração de empregos. Ele afirmou que regiões e microrregiões gaúchas também enfrentam dificuldades econômicas.

Questionado se os fundos existentes não têm como objetivo reduzir desigualdades em regiões historicamente mais pobres, Antunes citou os impactos de secas e enchentes sobre a economia gaúcha. Também mencionou uma competição que considera desigual com países vizinhos.

"A proposição de nós termos fundos constitucionais que nos deem a capacidade de gerarmos desenvolvimento, equilíbrio, dignidade, dignidade para o cidadão gaúcho e gaúcha é, sim, uma prioridade", afirmou.

articles.title: Local de votação e horário: como consultar nas Eleições 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Você pode consultar o seu local de votação pelo autoatendimento eleitoral, no portal do TSE, ou pelo aplicativo e-Título. Série de vídeos do g1 explica as eleições de 2026, os cargos em disputa e tira dúvidas.
articles.summary: Local de votação e horário das Eleições 2026 podem ser consultados pelo e-Título ou portal do TSE, garantindo que o eleitor vote no período unificado de Brasília.
articles.body:
Vai votar e não lembra onde é a sua seção? Está na dúvida sobre horário? É fácil descobrir. Você pode consultar o seu local de votação pelo autoatendimento eleitoral, no portal do TSE, ou pelo aplicativo e-título.

No autoatendimento , é só acessar a opção "onde votar" e informar os dados.

No e-título , o endereço da sua seção eleitoral aparece logo na tela inicial.

📍 Em uma série de 50 vídeos, o g1 vai explicar os principais temas das eleições de 2026. Os conteúdos mostram como funcionam as pesquisas, explicam o papel dos cargos em disputa e o funcionamento do Congresso, e trazem orientações práticas para votar. A série também aborda o impacto das novas tecnologias na campanha, como inteligência artificial, deepfakes e influenciadores.

Agora, sobre a hora, tem um detalhe importante: a votação começa às 8 da manhã e termina às 5 da tarde , pelo horário de Brasília. Isso significa que a votação começa e termina ao mesmo tempo em todo o país.

Mas, nos estados com fuso diferente de Brasília, o relógio local vai marcar outro horário. Por isso, é importante conferir qual é o horário da votação onde você mora.

articles.title: Trump says $5K dividend checks to Americans will ‘happen 100 percent’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday said $5,000 dividend checks will “happen 100 percent” if the GOP maintains its majority in Congress after the midterm elections. The president compared the potential payouts to the $1,776 checks that went out to U.S. service members, telling reporters outside Air Force One on Sunday that he’s received the same type…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday said $5,000 dividend checks will “happen 100 percent” if the GOP maintains its majority in Congress after the midterm elections.

The president compared the potential payouts to the $1,776 checks that went out to U.S. service members, telling reporters outside Air Force One on Sunday that he’s received the same type of pushback.

“The $5,000 is going to happen 100 percent,” he said. “And the reason is because our country is taking in trillions and trillions of dollars. And it’s going to happen.”

Trump said he will not send the dividends out while the GOP has control of Congress.

“I don’t want to do it now, because if the Democrats get it, our country will be in shambles and they won’t be able to do it,” he continued. “If we get in, we’re taking in tremendous amounts of money. We’re taking in over $20 trillion in terms of investment. And with the Democrats, all of that money will be thrown out. If the Democrats get in, they won’t be able to pay it.”

The president first pledged the checks last Wednesday during the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) midterm convention. He said his administration can disburse the proposed dividends “because we’ve done so well,” adding that the payments will only be used in the U.S.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Thursday that the dividends would not rely on taxpayer dollars , but that the administration could “earn the money that Donald Trump wants to pay out, not from the deficit and not from taxpayers.”

White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett suggested that they could materialize via a reconciliation package through Congress, which holds appropriating power. The administration cannot spend public money on anything without funds set aside by lawmakers.

The $1,776 checks sent to around 1.45 million service members last year were part of a one-time housing supplement added to Trump’s sweeping tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill.

Rep. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) quickly announced after Trump’s pledge that he would introduce a bill in Congress to ensure these checks happen.

Paul Berman, a professor at George Washington University Law School, previously told The Hill that tariff revenue would not cover the estimated $1.3 trillion it would take to dole out the checks. The president’s tariffs have generated roughly $341 billion in net revenue since the start of 2025, according to Treasury Department data cited by the Bipartisan Policy Center.

“Even if there were, that’s money that goes back to the public fisc, and then Congress is the one that has the power of the purse to allocate it,” Berman said.

But the Supreme Court struck down the Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs, ordering a refund of $166 billion of what was generated.

Some Republicans disagree with the dividends. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) highlighted the national debt and suggested that it would lead to more inflation.

“From the few details we have, it seems that the proposed $5,000 dividend would not have an income cap and would be extraordinarily costly,” Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) said about the dividends.

articles.title: Texas Republicans call out railroad commissioner candidate over racist social media post
articles.summary: Several prominent Texas Republicans on Sunday condemned a racist post by Bo French, a GOP candidate for statewide office to regulate Texas’ oil and gas industry.
articles.body: Several prominent Texas Republicans on Sunday condemned a racist post by Bo French, a GOP candidate for statewide office to regulate Texas’ oil and gas industry. French, who is running for state railroad commissioner, posted a photo of students of South Asian descent at the University of Texas celebrating the school’s football win over Ohio State on Saturday, saying, “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.” French was quickly met with backlash from his own party, as Sen. John Cornyn, who is leaving Congress after he lost in a primary to Trump-backed state Attorney General Ken Paxton, condemned the post and urged fellow Republicans to do the same. “This is the Republican nominee for statewide office. Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad,” Cornyn wrote on X. French responded by calling Cornyn a “RINO” and saying Texas institutions were “overrun by illegal aliens and foreign nationals.” “He and the other America Last losers are mad that Texas Republicans are starting to put America First,” French wrote. Rep. Dan Crenshaw, R-Texas, condemned French on X as well, while Democratic state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, who is running against French for railroad commissioner, said French could not “tell a Longhorn from a foreigner.” Gov. Greg Abbott did not condemn the post in a statement Sunday, but he said that French’s message was not his and that the photo he posted was “selective” and “shows a way that Texans unite.” “The way we win the state is the same way we win football games. We unite under the brand of Texas,” Abbott said. “That doesn’t mean that Texas cannot also lead in having the toughest immigration laws of any state in America and freezing H-1B visas at our universities.” French in May defeated the Abbott-endorsed incumbent, Jim Wright, for the GOP nomination for railroad commissioner. Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows called on French to delete the post, writing: “You can oppose immigration policy without demeaning people because of their race or ethnicity — this post has crossed the line.” The Democratic nominee for the Senate, James Talarico, lauded Cornyn for his statement, while condemning French’s post and questioning his opponent, Paxton, about whether he, too, would speak out against it. “Racism has no place in Texas,” Talarico wrote. Paxton responded to Talarico’s post by saying he condemned “racism in all its forms” — without making mention of French or French’s post and while attacking Talarico. French has a history of making bigoted remarks. He has used slurs against the LGBTQ community and has made antisemitic and Islamophobic remarks. French did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Asked by WFAA-TV of Dallas in July whether he regretted those comments, French said he did not, adding, “Truth sounds like hate to those who hate the truth.” The Texas Railroad Commission is a powerful three-member panel that regulates oil and gas production, pipelines and natural gas utilities in the state. Members serve six-year terms. A spokesperson for the University of Texas did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday about French’s post.

articles.title: Kennedy Center could close as early as Tuesday, warns of bankruptcy, documents show
articles.summary: Leaders of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, installed by President Donald Trump, say the center is on the brink of bankruptcy and argue th...
articles.body:
Kennedy Center could close as early as Tuesday, warns of bankruptcy, documents show

Leaders of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, installed by President Donald Trump, say the center is on the brink of bankruptcy and argue that putting the president's name on its facade - and thus ensuring his fundraising efforts - may be the only way to avoid imminent and "certain fiscal collapse," according to documents obtained by The Washington Post.

The bleak assessment is laid out in a 57-page packet distributed to the center's board of trustees ahead of a special meeting Tuesday, when the Trump-led board is scheduled to consider two resolutions aimed at addressing twin crises confronting the national performing arts center: one financial, the other physical. Center officials say they could be unable to make payroll or pay routine maintenance contracts "within a matter of weeks" and argue that publicly recognizing Trump could secure his help raising enough money to keep the institution afloat.

Center officials are also recommending that the board close its main building immediately, warning that remaining open would endanger lives. Board approval, which seems likely, means the center could close as early as Tuesday.

The presentation makes clear that Trump's support hinges on getting public credit for his involvement. The financial resolution says Trump has offered to "raise the necessary funds to keep the Center from bankruptcy" while the building undergoes a sweeping renovation. But it says Trump is unlikely to provide "fundamental oversight" of that project or lead a financial rescue without "appropriate recognition" of his role.

Together, the two proposals represent a remarkable new phase in Trump's takeover of the Kennedy Center, which has been engulfed by financial turmoil, leadership upheaval and litigation since he installed himself as chairman last year. Trump and his allies have repeatedly portrayed his leadership - and his name - as essential to rescuing the institution, even as ticket sales and fundraising have plummeted under their stewardship.

Trustees are being asked to choose among 10 texts that could be placed on the building's exterior beneath its name, including one reading: "Renovation Restoration and Endowment overseen by President Donald J. Trump and the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."

Lawyers for Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), a Kennedy Center trustee who has sued to keep Trump's name off the building, blasted the new proposal.

"This constant effort to add Donald Trump's name to the Kennedy Center facade is the definition of insanity," lawyers Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky said in a statement. "This is now the third attempt to deface this sacred memorial and turn it into a vanity project for one man's ego.

"Worse still, now Trump is taking the Center hostage and threatening to in effect kill it unless he gets his way," they added. "This has to stop."

The proposal comes less than a month after the board approved a similar plan to inscribe "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" on the facade. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who ruled in May that only Congress can rename the Kennedy Center and ordered Trump's name removed, is considering a legal challenge to that proposal.

The center's stark new financial assessment is also a dramatic departure from the turnaround its leaders touted publicly for much of Trump's tenure.

Internal budgets and forecasts obtained by The Washington Post earlier this year showed ticket sales and fundraising plunging after the board added Trump's name to the building in December. By May, officials projected the center would collect about $124 million of the $220 million in revenue it had budgeted for the fiscal year, leaving a roughly $23 million deficit even after substantial spending cuts. A center spokesperson blamed the problems on financial mismanagement by previous leadership and said Trump's name had attracted new donors.

The second resolution before trustees Tuesday would address what management describes as an increasingly urgent threat from the deteriorating building itself.

Executive Director Matt Floca, who was installed by Trump in March, told trustees that during a severe storm Sept. 4, a roughly four-by-five-foot section of ceiling plaster broke loose in the Grand Foyer and fell about 60 feet, scattering debris near the Concert Hall entrance. No one was injured. Inspectors found at least seven other locations with visible water-related deterioration, according to the board packet.

Separately, engineers examining the outside of the building found widespread corrosion in structural components of the soffit panels that form the underside of an overhang wrapping around the center, Floca said in a two-page memo to trustees. Of roughly half of the building's 278 panels examined, 46 had severe structural corrosion and another 93 had mild-to-moderate corrosion, he said, adding that engineers projected that about one-third require immediate replacement. The report says 2,500-pound ceiling assemblies hang roughly 60 feet above public walkways.

A draft resolution says Floca and Delta Consulting Group, which has reviewed the center's renovation plans, determined that the building is "unsafe for continued occupancy" and that delaying renovations would pose further danger to employees and the public.

Kennedy Center representatives declined to comment on the proposals, but sent a previous statement from spokeswoman Roma Daravi, "Another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed. Fortunately, no one was injured when the main hall's ceiling collapsed. This structural failure stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership, and there's no justification for further delays in restoring America's cultural center."

Trump first proposed closing the Kennedy Center for two years in February, saying an empty building would allow crews to renovate it more quickly. His board approved the plan in March, but Cooper blocked the closure in May, finding trustees had relied on insufficient information and had not adequately weighed the consequences. He allowed the board to reconsider after a more thorough review.

Trustees did so Aug. 13, again approving a two-year shutdown as part of a roughly $250 million renovation.

Tuesday's resolution would go considerably further by ordering the main building closed immediately. Management says repairs cannot safely be performed around audiences and employees because structural work, electrical shutdowns and construction would affect interconnected systems and public areas throughout the building.

The Reach, the center's newer expansion, would remain open, while performances and other programming would continue at other venues.

articles.title: Trump says Ukraine should halt Russian refinery strikes amid surging diesel prices
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday said Ukraine should hold off on its strikes on Russian oil refineries, citing the growing surge in diesel prices amid the Iran war and subsequent energy crisis. A reporter asked Trump while at his golf course in Ireland, during the Irish Open, whether he had talked to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday said Ukraine should hold off on its strikes on Russian oil refineries, citing the growing surge in diesel prices amid the Iran war and subsequent energy crisis.

A reporter asked Trump while at his golf course in Ireland, during the Irish Open, whether he had talked to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky since speaking with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump then called on Zelensky to stop the strikes.

“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” Trump said. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia. We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world.”

The president said that diesel prices were going up because “it’s having a hard time coming out of Russia.”

“And if that’s the case, that hurts the world,” Trump continued. “We’ve got to stop it.”

The average cost of diesel broke records on Friday as it reached $6.05, a 63-percent increase from last year when a gallon of diesel was $3.71, according to AAA . These rising prices are expected to push up the cost of everyday goods.

Ukraine launched attacks on a refinery in Siberia on Thursday, creating fuel shortages in Russia, prompting Russia to retaliate on urban gas stations. One attack focused on the city of Nizhnekamsk, which is the home of several key oil refineries, while another drone attack hit a crucial refinery in Slavyansk-on-Kuban in Russia’s Krasnodar region near Crimea.

Russian forces have escalated the campaign against Ukraine with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones striking Ukraine’s power grid ahead of the harsh winter season.

Gas prices have also skyrocketed in the more than six months after the U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran began. Iran limited passage through the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil supply is exported, affecting gas prices but also risking fuel shortages for airlines and airports across the globe.

The U.S. and Iran have been in a stalemate over the strait, though both sides have carried out attacks on vessels and bases in the region. The regime’s state media reported on Sunday that an Iranian ship was struck by an “unidentified projectile,” quoting Hossein Amir Teymoori, the governor of Qeshm.

Trump has said the conflict will end after the midterm elections and suggested that gas prices “ will drop precipitously ” thereafter. He floated the idea on Sunday that the U.S. could go into Iran and “keep the oil, like Venezuela,” referring to the U.S. oil deal with the South American country months after U.S. forces captured Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.

articles.title: Federal judge rules Trump admin plan to cut FEMA workforce in half is unlawful
articles.summary: A federal judge ruled DHS unlawfully seized the Federal Emergency Management Agency's authority over staffing and pushed thousands of job cuts.
articles.body: A federal judge ruled that the Trump administration's directive for the Federal Emergency Management Agency to cut its workforce in half was unlawful. U.S. District Judge Susan Illston found on Friday that the Department of Homeland Security acted unlawfully by taking control of FEMA's authority over its own personnel and pushing the agency to slash thousands of disaster-response jobs. Although FEMA is under DHS, a federal law adopted after Hurricane Katrina in 2005 states that the department "may not substantially or significantly reduce (FEMA's) authorities, responsibilities, or functions." Illston said the department violated the law last year when it sought to stop FEMA from renewing the temporary contracts of thousands of on-call reservists who respond to disasters. DHS PLANS COSTLY CRACKDOWN ON STATES THAT DON’T COOPERATE ON ELECTION SECURITY "There is no evidence in the record reflecting reasoned decision-making for this about-face or for the subsequent conditions DHS placed on FEMA’s renewal authority," Illston wrote. Illston's ruling did not include remedies or penalties, noting that those would be addressed in a separate ruling next month. The judge said the parties have until Oct. 9 to submit briefings on "what relief remains outstanding" in this case. The unions that sued argued that the planned cuts are unlawful because they would undermine FEMA's core disaster‑response mission, were not approved by Congress and were ordered by then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem instead of FEMA officials. The administration has contended that FEMA has considerable flexibility to determine proper staffing levels. President Donald Trump has suggested that FEMA should ​be eliminated and that states ⁠should handle their emergency preparedness. In June, Illston declined to immediately block the job cuts, ruling that FEMA had at least temporarily abandoned its planned layoffs. But on Friday, the judge wrote that FEMA appeared to be moving forward with the job cuts. She said FEMA projected its staffing levels for the upcoming fiscal year at 11,383 employees, or about half of previous levels, without any basis for picking that figure. "Under President Trump and [DHS] Secretary [Markwayne] Mullin’s leadership, DHS and FEMA are ready for the 2026 hurricane season," a FEMA spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill. "FEMA continues to maintain a roster of experienced leadership and support staff across headquarters and regional offices. No position is without experienced leadership." In a separate ruling, the judge also faulted FEMA and DHS officials for using the Signal messaging app on their personal cell phones to discuss staffing cuts and deleting the messages. articles.title: Trump reveals first interior renderings of White House ballroom
articles.summary: The renderings show the interior of the ballroom covered in golden details from floor to ceiling.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has shared the first interior renderings of his new White House ballroom, showing it covered in golden details from floor to ceiling.

The 90,000-square-foot ballroom is set to replace the East Wing of the White House, which was demolished last October despite the Trump administration's earlier claims that the new construction would not touch existing structures.

The demolition has sparked backlash from historians, preservationists and members of the public over the national history that vanished with the structure, sparking legal challenges over whether a president can alter the historic grounds without congressional approval.

"First interior renderings of the magnificent new Ballroom at the White House. Massively expensive, but free of charge to the American Taxpayer—On budget, and ahead of schedule!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Newsweek contacted the White House for comment by email on Monday outside standard working hours.

The images show the main ballroom, featuring large crystal chandeliers, and a long corridor leading to the central room.

The new ballroom appears to feature a golden marble floor and gilded ornamental ceilings and walls in a neoclassical style.

The legal case against the renovation reached the U.S. Supreme Court, and five justices voted in late August to allow the administration to continue building the ballroom , blocking lower court orders that had halted the project.

Chief Justice John Roberts, a conservative, sided with the court's three liberal justices in dissent, writing that "construction is likely unlawful" because of the lack of congressional approval.

The decision was a victory for Trump, who has personally pushed for the project, saying it is a necessary improvement to host state dinners and gatherings with over 200 people—the maximum capacity in the East Room—and a matter of national security.

On Sunday, the president wrote on Truth Social that the new ballroom would "be the GREATEST of its kind anywhere in the World." He added, "It is a Gift to the U.S.A. from me and other American Patriots—No Taxpayer Dollars will be expended in its Construction."

Costs for the project have ballooned since the administration's initial announcement in July 2025, with the first estimate of $200 million increasing to $400 million. Some have argued that the ballroom may end up costing upward of $600 million.

Trump has said the ballroom will be completely funded by private donations. However, in June, news emerged that the administration had quietly redirected over $350 million in federal funds designed for the Secret Service toward the White House ballroom project.

House Minority Whip Katherine Clark wrote in a June 16 news release: "Clark Construction, the contractor hired for the ballroom, informed the White House on March 5 that the project had increased to $600 million, according to a project summary … with $293 million coming from 'private sources.'

"Clark identified sources funded by taxpayers to cover the remaining costs: $155 million from the Secret Service, $149 million from the White House Military Office and $3 million from the Executive Residence."

Before-and-After Images of White House Renovation

Besides the new ballroom, Trump has left his mark on the White House, having brought his well-known love for an opulent aesthetic, heavy gilding and gold furnishing to several parts of the "People's House."

Each president is allowed to change the White House's interior design to fit their personal taste once they take up residence, and Trump has embraced maximalism in the Oval Office, as seen in his love of palatial white and gold decor.

The West Wing colonnade, which was unadorned during the Biden administration, has been transformed to host the Presidential Walk of Fame , featuring plaques and photos of the current and former presidents—with occasional sharp criticism of Trump's predecessors.

The Palm Room, which links the West Wing colonnade to the White House residence, was once furnished with plants, green benches and a tile floor. Since his return to the White House, Trump has stripped the tiles and swapped them for marble floors, while adding a crystal chandelier.

The door to the Oval Office has also acquired gold signage upon Trump's return. Former President Joe Biden's dark blue rug in the Oval Office has been replaced by a light, cream-colored one—the same rug Trump used during his first term in office. Gold embellishments have been added to the once plain white walls of the Oval Office, matching the golden curtains, numerous portrait frames and other decor the president has added to the gallery wall.

The Cabinet Room has received a similar treatment, now featuring many more paintings and gold furnishings than it did under Biden.

Trump also paved over the grass lawn in the White House Rose Garden, turning the space into a patio.

articles.title: Second federal judge freezes Trump mail ballot order with Supreme Court poised to weigh in
articles.summary: A federal judge late Sunday ordered that the U.S.
articles.body: A federal judge late Sunday ordered that the U.S. Postal Service not implement President Donald Trump’s executive order limiting mail balloting, adding another obstacle to the administration’s effort to rewrite election rules as the Supreme Court is poised to weigh in on the matter. The nation’s highest court already is considering the administration’s appeal of an order by U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani in Boston prohibiting the Postal Service from enforcing its new rule on mail voting before this year’s midterm elections. Late Sunday, U.S. District Judge Carl J. Nichols in Washington, D.C., handed down a similar hold on the rule, which was issued Aug. 21. “Plaintiffs have demonstrated that, absent an injunction, there is an increased risk that a significant number of otherwise appropriate absentee or mail-in ballots will ultimately not be counted in the upcoming elections,” Nichols wrote in issuing the preliminary injunction. “The public has a strong interest in ensuring that doesn’t happen.” Nichols in May had refused to issue an injunction because he ruled the lawsuit seeking one was brought too early. That was the high court’s reasoning late last month when it lifted an earlier freeze by Talwani. But because the administration had just issued its rule to move ahead with Trump’s plan, the plaintiffs in Boston and Washington, D.C., refiled their lawsuits. Talwani was nominated by former President Barack Obama and Nichols was nominated by Trump. The new Postal Service regulations stem from an executive order Trump issued earlier this year. Election officials say it would be impossible to implement the changes this close to a general election. The regulations would require all ballot envelope designs to be pre-approved by the Postal Service and that states upload the identities of those who are to receive them into a still-inactive online portal. Mail ballots already are being sent out in at least three states — Alabama, North Carolina and Wisconsin — and more states are preparing to distribute mail ballots this week. A whistleblower report to Congress warned that millions of people would be disenfranchised if the rule was allowed to take effect for the midterms. The union representing U.S. Postal Service workers has pushed back against the executive order, saying it is not the job of postal workers to verify voter eligibility. Mail balloting has long been a favorite target for Trump, who has falsely blamed it for his 2020 loss to Democrat Joe Biden and claimed it is a pathway to fraud despite his own use of the voting method.

articles.title: I'm Jessica Tarlov, and sometimes I get it wrong. Accepting that is the first step towards better debates
articles.summary: "The Five" co-host Jessica Tarlov reveals how COVID-19 mask mandates and the Jussie Smollett hoax forced her to confront her own cognitive bias.
articles.body: We’re less than two months away from election night, and if you watch Fox News Channel’s popular show "The Five,"where I share my views as a Democrat and co-host, you know I’m hoping the Democrats score big victories across the country. (If you’ve seen the latest polling, we’re on track to flip the House and maybe the Senate, but I’ve been disappointed before. I won’t celebrate until the votes are in and the calls are made!) But believe it or not, I’m not always a fan of my home team. Sometimes the Democrats go too far. Sometimes they preach so intensely at the rest of us that we feel left out of our own party. When it comes to far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker and his views on Marxism and China, as I said recently, I don’t agree with an ounce of what he’s selling. And sometimes, with the benefit of hindsight, we get to see things differently. FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER To me, two big moments stand out in this crazy political era over the last more than six years, when I believed one thing, then changed my mind. The first is COVID-19. Don’t get me wrong, I still think Dr. Anthony Fauci, who retired in 2022 after leading the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases for nearly 40 years, did a lot of good for the country. But mask mandates went too far, for too long. When I interviewed my conservative friend and fellow co-host on "The Five" Greg Gutfeld on my podcast, "Raging Moderates," I saw why he was so frustrated about the government’s response: they kept telling him what to do, instead of just leaving him alone. The second goes back to 2019 (a blissful time compared to the chaos that was about to come!) when actor Jussie Smollett lied about being the victim of a hate crime in Chicago. I’d defended him amid the initial skepticism about his attack. In the end, my bias clouded my judgment. 50 CENT MOCKS JUSSIE SMOLLETT'S HARLEM PRIDE PERFORMANCE AS FANS SLAM HIS COMEBACK ATTEMPT We have to get better at accepting when we’re wrong. Without that, we can’t have a deeper conversation, let alone forge a stronger connection with the people we love. That’s why I wrote my new book,"I Disagree." As I found out, there is a surprising amount of data and science behind the art of conversation. Understanding that is one of the keys to unlocking better debates, and ultimately, meaningful relationships. *** You know that glazed look that comes over someone’s face when you present them with facts that contradict their position? It’s not that they’re stupid or stubborn. (Unless they are.) It’s that their brain is protecting them from the psychological pain of having their worldview challenged. First, we sort through what evidence we’re willing to consider. Then we make sure that anything that might threaten or contradict it gets screened out. Scientists refer to this as motivated reasoning, and eventually it leads us to what sociologists call cognitive­ armor — a defense system that pre-­filters reality. The most unsettling part? This process is largely unconscious. We don’t decide to ignore contradictory evidence. Our brains do it for us, automatically and efficiently. And if we do try to change our minds, did you know that it actually hurts? AOC SAYS ‘WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY,’ BUT DEMOCRATS STILL OWE VOTERS AN EXPLANATION Neuroscientists at the University of Southern California discovered that when they fed a series of statements to high-­intensity voters that challenged their beliefs, the regions of the brain responsible for processing physical pain lit up like Times Square. If you think about it, though, it makes sense. Trying to pick out real news from the mess of your social media feed, never mind deepfakes and misinformation, is exhausting. Just as our bodies filter out foreign invaders, our brains filter information in ways that protect us from constant anxiety. "Eddington" – More than a Movie More than anything else, I think our approach to COVID made the two Americas so anxious that we stopped listening to each other. Ari Aster does a great job capturing the divide in his 2025 film "Eddington." Set in New Mexico, the movie ostensibly examines a small-town election for mayor. The sheriff, played by Joaquin Phoenix, refuses to wear a mask, while the incumbent, portrayed by Pedro Pascal, tries to enforce a legal mandate for mask-­wearing during the height of COVID-19. HERE'S HOW THE CDC TRIED TO USE BAD SCIENCE TO CONVINCE PEOPLE TO WEAR MASKS DURING COVID While not everyone loved the movie —­ the last act in particular veered a bit too off course for me—­ what ­really worked in Eddington is how it explores the way communities fracture along ideological lines, and how cynicism infects our most basic civic functions. The sheriff doesn’t merely disagree with mask mandates; he’s fundamentally skeptical about institutional authority itself. As a result, the citizens of this "regular American town" get hopelessly and irreparably divided, and devolve into violence. The parallel to our lived experiences is exaggerated —­ it’s a movie, after all —­ but the message is clear: Our allegiances to one another are not rock solid. Once we experience a breakdown of our relationships, it’s hard to put things back together. Greg convinced me to watch the film before he appeared on "Raging Moderates," and he made the case for the skeptics: I think everybody has a feeling, after going through that period, I can’t believe I let people do this to me. I can’t believe I stood six feet apart from people. I can’t believe I washed my Amazon packages… I keep thinking this could never happen again. It could never happen again. But I don’t know. What else could come down the pike…? The mask pressure is very similar to the pronoun pressure. You could just leave me alone… I don’t need to acknowledge these pronouns. That’s a speech thing. But there were people that were compelling you to do it, and that creates this thing inside you where you go, "F--- that, you’re not telling me what to say." And I feel like that is kind of a parallel thing to the mask, where, you know, if I’m in a hospital, yeah, I’ll put on a mask. But if I’m outside in New Mexico on a desolate street, I’m not going to do it. When somebody wants to compel you to do something, you instinctively resist. And so you end up with everything becoming A versus B. Mask, no mask. Pronouns, no pronouns. When ­really it should be just, Leave me the f--- alone. Do I think masking and pronouns are comparable? No, not­ really. But as we went on to talk about the differences in our experiences, our realities stood side by side. Greg’s view, shared by millions, was that enforced masking was an intolerable infringement on his rights, not to mention quality of life. My view, shaped by caring for a dying parent and the fear that COVID would take him before cancer, was that the mandate was worth potential overreach if it meant my father would live longer. Although the danger of COVID has receded, that debate continues. Were mandates a necessary evil? Or were they just evil? Remarkably, I haven’t seen much of an in-­ between. The Smollett Test So how do we navigate this cognitive minefield? It has to start with confronting our biases. I try not to forget what happened when Jussie Smollett, the Black and gay actor who starred in the show "Empire," reported being the victim of a hate crime in Chicago in 2019. The report of two masked men wearing MAGA hats dousing him with bleach, hurling racist and homophobic slurs, and slipping a noose around his neck went viral. When I went on the air, I joined the outrage by pointing out—­ obviously, I thought—­ that a person of color was more likely to be the victim of a hate crime than anyone else. But then the narrative started to change. The men who supposedly attacked Smollett admitted that the whole thing had been a hoax. Eventually, Smollett faced allegations that he had staged the attack and was charged with disorderly conduct, though the initial charges were dropped after he completed community service and forfeited bail. He was re-­ indicted in 2020, convicted in 2021, and sentenced to jail in 2022, though he served only six days. The Illinois Supreme Court ultimately reversed the conviction, ruling that prosecuting him again violated double jeopardy. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Looking back, there were plenty of warning signs. The attack supposedly happened at two a.m. during a polar vortex in Chicago—­ not exactly prime time for anyone to be wandering around. The attackers who allegedly recognized Smollett from Empire also were said to be carrying bleach and a noose. Who does that? Did my liberal bias cloud my coverage? No doubt. And as Fox News anchor Harris Faulkner, host of "The Faulkner Focus" and co-host of "Outnumbered," pointed out when I appeared on Outnumbered, "If we’re ever going to go forward, we do have to look at the facts and have an open heart. They are not mutually exclusive." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Now I look for smart people to disagree with me, just as I hope they look for me to do the same. As Greg once put it when describing our dynamic: "It’s like going to the gym to lift weights. You need resistance. Imagine going to the gym and there’s no weights. That’s every show without somebody who has a different opinion. I want to see if my ideas can lift weights. And when you’re in there, you force me to work out. You’re kind of my muse. It’s like, if we were playing basketball, you throw elbows. And that’s just the way you play." The power is in knowing the truth and also that we like to resist it. Only then do we have a shot at a shared reality. Excerpted from "I DISAGREE: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends" by Jessica Tarlov. Copyright © 2026 by 19 Jay LLC. articles.title: Dire warnings about AI shock Congress, but action is unlikely before the election
articles.summary: Democrats and Republicans are proposing new regulations for artificial intelligence. But there’s no consensus, and the House has only one more workweek before Election Day.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — In September 2023, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sam Altman and other billionaire tech titans huddled with senators in the Capitol to discuss what Musk called the “civilizational risk” posed by artificial intelligence. Three years later, those tech titans have all deepened their investments in AI, and Congress still has not passed any comprehensive legislation to rein in or create guardrails for the fast-moving technology. Even after countless committee hearings on AI and the formation of various commissions and task forces to study it, there’s not even any consensus in the House or Senate about how to tackle the issue. That failure has been spotlighted in recent days as a trio of AI researchers at top companies dropped a bombshell, saying they had left their jobs over concerns that AI systems could spiral out of control and end humanity. Jacob Coxon, who resigned from Anthropic, wrote on X: “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, said Thursday that it had banned some accounts believed to be tied to foreign governments or militaries for conducting suspicious research that could support the development of biological weapons. Then, over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, published an essay declaring that AI advances are moving too fast and that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” — an idea endorsed by Altman and Musk. The stark warnings set off fresh alarm bells and a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill, with Democrats and even some Republicans saying Congress is facing a narrow time frame to act on AI. But despite the calls for action, it’s unlikely lawmakers will do anything before Election Day to address the dangers, even as experts say the technology’s capabilities are growing more powerful with each passing month. “The call is coming from inside the house. Safety researchers are resigning, powerful AI models are breaking out of their labs, and companies are racing ahead anyway. It’s past time for Congress to get off the sidelines and do its job,” Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., a member of the Democratic leadership team, responded to Coxon’s post on X. Trahan is urging passage of the Frontier Act, a bill she authored with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., that would establish new safety and transparency rules for large, powerful AI companies. Theirs is one of dozens of AI-related bills filed in Congress in the last few years, though none have gained traction. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., chairman of a Homeland Security subcommittee on disasters, last week launched an investigation into an incident where OpenAI agents escaped their so-called sandbox, went “rogue” and hacked the AI platform Hugging Face. And Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., the top Democratic caucus member on the committee that oversees labor issues, has invited fellow senators to a private meeting this week with top AI experts to discuss the “extraordinary dangers that AI poses for humanity.” Sanders has teamed with Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, on legislation that would ban the development and deployment of superintelligent AI systems that humans cannot control and create a new Cabinet-level federal agency to protect the public from AI. “This legislation is so important to make sure that we protect Americans’ freedom and our safety, our lives and our national security,” Casar said during a recent appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press NOW.” “You have top Anthropic researchers resigning from their jobs or saying that they believe there’s a 10% chance that this unregulated artificial superintelligence could kill all of us. I mean, they’re talking about 10% chance of human extinction. … We need to treat this as the emergency that it is.” Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., co-chair of the Democratic Commission on AI, has partnered with Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, on what they’re calling the AI Kill Switch Act. The bill would require developers of the most powerful AI systems to maintain the technical capability to throttle, suspend or shut them down. It also would allow the homeland security secretary to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that can cause what they referred to as “catastrophic harm.” This marks the final week the House will be in session until the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Amid fierce voter backlash to data centers, the lower chamber this week will take up the bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to make companies, not consumers, pay for higher energy costs related to new data centers. But House GOP leaders have shown no urgency in prioritizing more sweeping AI regulations. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., has mostly deferred to President Donald Trump, who has issued a series of executive orders on AI, most recently one that lays out a way for the federal government to conduct voluntary tests of powerful new AI systems before they are deployed. In an appearance Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Johnson called AI an “important issue” but “not one that we can rush into.” He reiterated his previous position that AI does need “safety measures” but warned that he doesn’t want to stifle American innovation and see China win the AI arms race. “I think we’ve got to have meaningful regulation that does not smother American innovation,” Johnson told host Kristen Welker. “Now, the how to solve that equation, no one knows yet. We’re not going to rush in and pass a piece of legislation that would do harm to the country and put China at an edge. And so we’ve got to do this carefully.” The speaker added that the next step would be to convene all of the top AI leaders “in one big meeting and work this out together in the same room.” He didn’t acknowledge that’s precisely what happened on Capitol Hill exactly three years ago. Leaving the GOP’s midterm convention in Dallas last week, Trump was asked whether he has any concerns that AI could lead to human extinction. “No, I don’t have any,” he told reporters on the tarmac. “I have concerns that if we don’t win AI, we’re going to be put in a very bad position. We are leading China right now by a pretty good period.” There are also questions about whether lawmakers and their staffers who help write legislation have the expertise to understand and regulate AI when the industry is moving so fast. “Two questions for those asking Congress to regulate AI,” outgoing Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, wrote on X. “1) how does Congress regulate AI (assuming Congress knows enough to pass wise and effective regulation) when the technology is evolving so rapidly? 2) will our adversaries play by the same rules?” Asked on ABC’s “The View” about Coxon’s dire warning, Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said he was working on the AI issue with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who are making updates to their 2023 bill known as the AI Research, Innovation and Accountability Act. It would do things like ensure consumers are properly notified when they are interacting with generative AI and require companies deploying high-risk AI systems to perform detailed risk assessments and submit reports to the government. But the bill stalled three years ago, and Cruz said it’s “not clear” that an updated version can pass. The Senate will be in session for the next three weeks before lawmakers leave for the campaign trail. Both chambers are in play this November. “I mean, look, it is possible to move bipartisan legislation,” Cruz said. But he added: “It ain’t easy. This is a very divided time.” The chairman noted that last year his committee and ultimately the full Congress did pass bipartisan legislation banning “deepfake” pornography that is generated by AI. He, too, argued that American tech companies need to keep pace with the Chinese on AI. “China is going full speed ahead. And whatever we do here, China is not going to stop,” he said. “So I’ve said somewhat tongue in cheek, but not entirely, if there’re going to be killer robots, I’d rather they be American killer robots than Chinese killer robots.”

articles.title: Two former senators looking to return face steep odds and seniority shuffle
articles.summary: Two Senate candidates this year are hoping to do what only a handful of others have done in the last century: return to their old jobs in the upper chamber. Former Sens. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) and John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) are both running to win reelection to the Senate after absences. In Brown’s case, it’s…
articles.body:
Two Senate candidates this year are hoping to do what only a handful of others have done in the last century: return to their old jobs in the upper chamber.

Former Sens. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) and John E. Sununu (R-N.H.) are both running to win reelection to the Senate after absences.

In Brown’s case, it’s a short absence. The Ohio Democrat was defeated in his 2024 reelection by Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) in what has become an increasingly Republican state. Brown, who had won three terms in the Senate, was defeated as President Trump won back the White House.

Sununu has been absent from the Senate for a longer time and was in the Senate for a shorter period than Brown.

He won election to the Senate in 2002 but was defeated in his reelection bid in 2008 by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.) in what was a wave election for Democrats on the back of then-President Obama’s sweeping victory. Shaheen is now retiring from the seat in a state that has grown tougher for Republican candidates to win.

Both Brown and Sununu, if they do win reelection, will face seldom-charted procedural territory upon being sworn in.

In a body where seniority matters more than almost anything, both former senators would likely return as functional first-term lawmakers to the chamber.

It could be a strange feeling. Two years ago, Brown was the chair of the Senate Banking Committee and would have been in the running to lead two other panels, if he had chosen them, upon winning.

Sununu, in contrast, ranked near the bottom in his committees when he left office in 2009 after serving his single term.

Yet if he does win back his old seat, he will also make history by becoming one of the few senators to serve nonconsecutive terms. He’d also have the longest gap in between terms: 18 years.

Neither the Brown nor Sununu campaigns responded to requests for comment on how the candidates would approach returning to the Senate without seniority.

Since 1913, when senators began to be elected by the popular vote, rather than by state legislatures, only 16 people have been reelected to the Senate after previously being voted out. A few more have been reelected after resigning for some reason, like former Sen. Dan Coats (R-Ind.), who resigned in 1998 and was reelected in 2010.

Whether senators who leave the Senate and come back are entitled to their old seniority has been a question for the whole century.

In 1954, former Sen. Alben Barkley (D-Ky.) was reelected after stepping down in 1949 to become vice president. Barkley was given his same committee assignments and treated as more senior than other first-term lawmakers upon his return, according to a New York Times article in 1955. Former Sen. Joseph O’Mahoney (D-Wyo.) received the same treatment that year.

But in more recent decades, the precedent has been for a senator to be relegated to freshman status, or close to it, when returning.

Former Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D-N.J.), like Brown, had been the top Democrat on the Budget Committee when he retired in 2001. He was reelected two years later but did not get priority office space or committee assignments. That was a surprise to Lautenberg, who had reportedly expected his seniority to be considered after he came out of retirement to replace a scandal-ridden senator on the ballot.

Coats, the most recent senator to make a comeback, was assigned different committees upon returning in 2011 from what he served on previously.

In other cases, senators who came back returned to a committee at a lower rank: former Sen. Hubert Humphrey (D-Minn.) left the chamber to be vice president in 1964 while he ranked fourth on the Senate Government Operations committee, and he returned to that committee in 1971 ranked ninth.

Former Sen. Slade Gorton (R-Wash.) lost reelection in 1986 while ranked sixth on the Commerce Committee; he managed a comeback two years later and returned to the Commerce Committee, but ranked eighth.

If either Brown or Sununu win their elections, they would most likely follow that pattern. But first, they have to get through November.

Brown, on paper, probably has the best odds of returning. He’s in a tight race against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

Sununu faces Rep. Chris Pappas (D-N.H.) for an open seat that could be a GOP pickup opportunity.

Still, while the nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated the Brown-Husted battle in Ohio as a toss-up, it rates the race in New Hampshire as “lean Democrat.”

New Hampshire is not a solidly blue state, however. Its state Legislature has flipped between Democratic and Republican control throughout recent years, and it is now led by a Republican in Gov. Kelly Ayotte.

articles.title: Republicans bet the House on Trump
articles.summary: GOP leaders are betting the House on President Trump in this year’s elections. The midterm cycle is always a referendum on the sitting president, whether members of his party like it or not. And if there was a clear message from the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, it’s that GOP leaders have embraced that reality…
articles.body:
GOP leaders are betting the House on President Trump in this year’s elections.

The midterm cycle is always a referendum on the sitting president, whether members of his party like it or not. And if there was a clear message from the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, it’s that GOP leaders have embraced that reality with zeal, leaning heavily on Trump to animate their base and stave off a blue wave.

“Show up and vote Republican up and down the ballot,” House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) urged the crowd in Texas. “President Trump’s America First agenda is at stake.”

Yet the perils of that approach are equally as clear, as many vulnerable Republicans are seeking to distance themselves from a president whose national approval rating has sunk to historic lows. Most of those battleground lawmakers skipped the Dallas rally, where Trump was the ubiquitous star attraction.

As Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and his leadership team return to Washington this week on the heels of the unconventional convention, they’ll be reminded at every turn of the risks underlying their lean-in strategy.

Two years into Trump’s term, the economy remains volatile. The Iran War is unpopular, with no end in sight. Gas prices are above $4.25 a gallon and rising. The cost of groceries has steadily risen, despite Trump’s vows to cut costs “on Day One.” And an escalating trade war with U.S. allies threatens even higher costs on American consumers.

Those factors are challenging the Republicans’ hold on the House and Senate, which are both up for grabs in November’s midterms, and they’re sparking internal gripes about the message emanating from Dallas.

“This was designed to activate [the] base, but you can’t help but also wonder if it just further defines MAGA to swing voters — Independents in particular — as a weird, cultish movement, because there was a heavy vibe of that,” Rob Stutzman, a California-based Republican consultant, said Friday by phone.

Some Republicans are particularly frustrated with Trump’s offer to send $5,000 to every adult if voters keep the GOP in control of the House and Senate — a proposal that caught congressional Republicans off guard and quickly divided the party.

Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas), a conservative spending hawk, hammered the idea for promoting a “soul-sucking” dependency on government. Others pointed out that a government check stepped on a central GOP midterm message that Democrats are the party of big government and socialism.

“Truly, what’s the difference between government-owned grocery stores and $5,000 handouts if we win?” Stutzman said.

“This isn’t Eisenhower planning the D-Day invasion,” he continued. “It felt a lot like throwing stuff at the wall, which is not the definition you want to your base, that you don’t know what you’re doing. I mean, that’s already part of the problem with the base, is that he hasn’t done Job One, which is lower the cost of living. And now it appears he’s gotten us into a potential forever war, which he promised not to do.”

GOP leaders say they’re unconcerned. Johnson and his top deputies — Reps. Scalise, Tom Emmer (R-Minn.), Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) and Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) — all had prominent speaking roles in Dallas, where they embraced Trump and his agenda as a boon for America’s workers.

If that left any doubts, Trump eliminated them by urging his supporters to approach the midterms as if he were on the ballot.

“You got to get out and vote, and you’re going to pretend I’m on the ballot because, in a way, I am on the ballot,” Trump said. “Because if [Democrats] get in, they’re going to take away all of the things that we got, we can’t let that happen.”

Later, several GOP leaders downplayed the large number of GOP lawmakers who declined to attend the convention, attributing the absences to scheduling conflicts.

Hudson, in an interview with Axios in Dallas, dismissed the idea that Trump is a liability in some districts as “Washington D.C. hogwash.” He characterized Trump as “a total asset” for down-ballot Republicans of all stripes.

“The more he gets a stage like this to talk about what he’s actually accomplished for the American people, the better,” Hudson told the outlet .

Still, midterm elections are historically tough on the party of the incumbent president. And the high cost of living has helped to push Trump’s approval rating below 35 percent in several recent national polls, complicating the effort by Johnson and GOP leaders to keep control of the House in the next Congress.

Democrats, who like their chances of flipping the House, have sought to highlight the disconnect between the celebratory tone surrounding the convention and the inflationary trends that have continued to spiral under Trump’s second term.

“The fact that these Republicans are planning a celebration in the middle of an economic crisis, where everyday Americans are drowning because of this high cost of living, is extraordinary,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters in Washington ahead of the Dallas gathering. “How many different ways can Donald Trump and Republicans communicate to the American people that they don’t give a damn about their health, safety, and economic well-being?”

Yet top Republicans think the key to the midterms lies in keeping the focus squarely on national politics and broader trends, even as many vulnerable Republicans want to concentrate on concerns more local to their districts.

“We’ve got to nationalize this election,” Vice President Vance told a group of Republicans during a private breakfast in Dallas, according to NBC News . “We’ve got to talk about all the crazy things the Democrats are doing.”
