articles.title: Republicans, fearing voter anger about costs, clash over economic strategy
articles.summary: Republicans are clashing over how to improve their weak polling numbers on the economy less than two months before Election Day, fearing that voter anger over high costs could sink GOP candidates in November. The boldest proposal, President Trump’s pledge to give every U.S. adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterm election, has already drawn…
articles.body:
Republicans are clashing over how to improve their weak polling numbers on the economy less than two months before Election Day, fearing that voter anger over high costs could sink GOP candidates in November.

The boldest proposal, President Trump’s pledge to give every U.S. adult $5,000 if Republicans win the midterm election, has already drawn strong pushback from Republicans across the political spectrum.

Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) says he would support the idea if the $5,000 payout is structured as a tax refund, but he warned that it should only go to people who work and pay taxes.

“I think we should be incentivizing work. I don’t think we should be paying people that are not working,” he argued.

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), however, warned it would be “extraordinarily costly” and questioned Trump’s idea of paying out thousands of dollars to people who don’t have financial need.

Some Republicans are pushing for quick action on other legislation to address costs, such as passing the stalled farm bill or capping credit card fees, but there’s little time to do anything before Election Day.

A Senate Republican strategist said there’s growing alarm among Republicans in Congress that the economic picture is not going to improve between now and Election Day, setting off a scramble among GOP candidates to pitch more ideas to bring down costs.

“Affordability and the war in Iran are going to continue on. They’re tied to each other. As long as the war in Iran continues, we will have high energy prices that will bleed over to consumers,” the strategist warned. “It just is a bad recipe.”

But getting the party on the same page about how to respond to the crisis has been a difficult task.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.), who is facing a surprisingly tough challenge from Democrat megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, is pushing his Credit Card Competition Bill, which he says would cut fuel and grocery prices by 2 or 3 percent by putting an end to what he calls the Visa-Mastercard “duopoly.”

Marshall says his bill, which Trump endorsed during the midterm convention in Dallas last week, would save Americans $1,200 a year.

“We’ll cut out-of-control credit card swipe fees, saving the average family at least $1,200 per year,” Trump declared on Wednesday.

But the proposal is facing stiff opposition from fellow Republicans on the Senate Banking Committee, according to a source familiar with the internal Senate dynamic.

The Senate is scheduled to be in session for only three more weeks before senators leave Washington again for the election and the House is planning only one week of work before lawmakers return to the campaign trail.

The average price of gasoline nationwide, which hit $4.30 a gallon on Friday, is sparking alarm among GOP candidates.

“That’s a problem,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), who is up for re-election and faces a tougher challenge than expected, according to recent Democratic polling.

“People need to bring the price of gas down. We all know that and we’re going to do everything we can to see that that happens,” he said.

Rounds said gas prices could come down 30 percents per gallon if Congress passed legislation to permanently allow the sale of gasoline blended with higher amounts of ethanol — E15 — nationwide.

He noted the E15 provision in the farm bill, which Senate Republicans are hoping to advance out of the Agriculture Committee once Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) returns to work from a protracted absence.

But Republicans from oil-producing states such as Texas, Oklahoma and Louisiana, which have mid-size refineries, have pushed back against allowing more E15 blended fuel onto the market.

Trump’s efforts to intervene in the economy has also provoked dissention on Capitol Hill, especially his decision to allow the import of 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef to reduce ground beef prices at the grocery store.

That move sparked an angry backlash from GOP senators from farm and ranching states who argued that flooding the market with cheaper imports would undercut cattlemen at a time when the farm economy is struggling to cope with high fuel costs and low commodity prices.

“Every time the government micromanages the economy, the consumer suffers,” warned Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who dismissed some of Trump’s interventions as “gimmicks.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s intervention in the bond market to lower yields and consumer borrowing costs has gotten a skeptical response from some Republicans on Capitol Hill.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to its highest level in three years after the Treasury Department announced it would repurchase $6 billion in 10- to 20-year government bonds, a market reaction that was interpreted as a rebuke from investors.

There are other worrisome signals that the country’s economic picture won’t improve substantially by Election Day.

The Consumer Price Index report released Friday showed that inflation is rising at an annual rate of 3.4 percent, well above the Federal Reserve’s target and faster than the rate of annual wage growth, which stands at 3.1 percent last month, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Meanwhile, the price of oil is hovering around $100 a barrel after rising by nearly 10 percent last week amid escalating strikes between U.S. and Iranian forces.

An Economist/YouGov poll of 1,536 adults conducted from Aug. 21 to Aug. 24 found that only 28 percent of Americans are satisfied with the economy while 64 percent are dissatisfied.

The poll showed that Democrats have a 7-point lead over Republicans on the question of which party does a better job on economic issues. It found 39 percent of Americans think the Democratic Party is stronger on the economy while 32 percent think Republicans are better on that issue.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), who has repeatedly expressed concern over the impact of high gas prices on his constituents, has introduced a bill to suspend the 18-cent federal gas tax, something Trump said he supported earlier this year.

But the idea has gotten slapped down by other Republican senators.

“I hate taxes, I wish that there weren’t a gas tax but I also like driving on the road. It’s a huge amount of money that just quits coming in,” Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) said in May, when Hawley unveiled his bill.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has questioned how to make up any shortfall in the Highway Trust Fund created by suspending the federal gas tax and voiced preference instead for reopening the Strait of Hormuz to shipping traffic.

Hawley in July also introduced legislation to send rebate checks to working Americans that would provide at least $600 per adult and dependent child.

He notes that the United States was projected to collect over $150 billion tariff revenue in 2025 alone.

But that proposal has also largely stalled because of Republican opposition in the Senate.

Several Republicans have raised concerns about the $40 trillion national debt, which is being blamed for rising Treasury yields and upward pressure on mortgage rates.

They argue money from Trump’s tariff regime should go toward reducing the annual federal deficit, which is projected to exceed $2 trillion in fiscal year 2026.

articles.title: LSU’s Lane Kiffin tests the NCAA’s limits, creating college football firestorm
articles.summary: Louisiana State University head coach Lane Kiffin quickly became the face of what many argue is wrong with modern college sports as the college football season approached this summer. The 51-year-old expert recruiter and protégé of University of Alabama legend Nick Saban had ditched his former playoff-bound school Ole Miss for an in-conference rival. He…
articles.body:
Louisiana State University head coach Lane Kiffin quickly became the face of what many argue is wrong with modern college sports as the college football season approached this summer.

The 51-year-old expert recruiter and protégé of University of Alabama legend Nick Saban had ditched his former playoff-bound school Ole Miss for an in-conference rival.

He was boasting about LSU’s deep name, image and likeness (NIL) budget, was luring elite student-athletes to Baton Rouge and was flirting with adding NFL rookies who had been cut by their professional teams to LSU’s roster.

After LSU was threatened with expulsion from the SEC and sued by the league over Kiffin’s offseason recruiting methods, the coach backed off, agreeing last week not to add former pro players to his team.

But a growing number of people around college football are pointing to Kiffin’s tactics as emblematic of what they see as a lack of fairness in college sports.

Kiffin’s bending of the NCAA and SEC’s eligibility rules, these people say, is the result of an intensifying arms race that federal lawmakers are setting their sights on regulating as part of their agenda when they return to the Capitol this week.

“We’re reading all about how Lane Kiffin is a bad actor here, and he’s certainly being painted as such, but it’s a hell of a thing when these coaches are just following court orders. When a [judge] says you can play, I don’t think we’ve ever been in a situation like this,” said Rick Hamilton, an antitrust attorney specializing in student-athlete rights and eligibility. “It’s just common sense. If you know what other [schools] can do and you’re competing against them … this is big business.”

Arguably the hottest debate in college sports today, the controversy at LSU centers on players in the class of 2022 who declared for the NFL in the offseason but did not make pro rosters.

Several of them sued the NCAA over its newly implemented “five seasons in five years” rule, arguing they should be able to take advantage of the rule retroactively and return to college competition.

Three players who Kiffin had been eyeing sued in Louisiana this summer and won, clearing the way for them to be legally added to rosters of college teams in the state.

Kiffin contended the players were fair game to recruit under the NCAA’s and Southeastern Conference’s guidelines and warned if LSU did not seek to add them, another school would.

“The players chose us. A lot of people were recruiting them, a lot of people were offering them a lot of money,” Kiffin said on a recent episode of Pat McAfee’s ESPN program. “So, we were happy, but we realize this [pushback] was going to come with it.”

Critics have blasted the LSU coach, arguing he is taking advantage of the NCAA’s recent struggles to enforce its eligibility rules, something the association has sought the help of Congress in strengthening.

If left unchecked, experts and observers say, more coaches are likely to continue taking spots away from currently enrolled students who, in many cases, have been with the team for years to free space for players with some professional experience.

“I don’t think he’s going to be the last coach to do this. Because of where we are in college sports with NIL and the loose transfer rules, coaches are under so much pressure now to build their rosters and find talent wherever they can,” said Jim Johnson, a sports business expert and attorney. “For players, coaches, scouts and everyone involved, the business of college sports is no longer in the back of their minds, it’s driving the decisionmaking.”

Kiffin seems to be relishing the controversy his recruiting methods have sparked.

During a brief television interview after the Tigers built a sizable first-half lead against Clemson University in Week 1, the LSU coach quipped, “Imagine if we were allowed to have the NFL players,” as he ran into a tunnel leading to the team’s locker room.

A leaked video from the LSU locker room minutes later caught him using outside chatter around the program to motivate his players, screaming, “The whole f‑‑‑ing world hates you! So you get a chance to show the world go f‑‑‑ yourself!”

Those comments led the Southeastern Conference to amend its lawsuit days later, making reference to Kiffin’s quote and arguing he was showing a reckless disregard for the integrity of college sports.

“He’s having fun with it. He thinks this is entertaining,” said college football pundit Paul Finebaum, who earlier this year considered a run for Senate in Alabama, during an episode of his talk show this week. “Maybe I’m too serious about following rules, but I don’t find any humor in Lane Kiffin, and I don’t know anybody outside of Louisiana that does.”

Inside Louisiana, Kiffin and his tactics have sturdy support, including from some who represent the state on Capitol Hill.

“LSU hasn’t done anything wrong. It’s called a court of law,” Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told reporters last week. “Now whether you agree with what LSU did or not, we did the right thing by going to court. And we’re going to follow the law, but they’re [the Southeastern Conference] not going to do anything if I have something to say about it.”

The controversy comes at a tense time for the conference and NCAA, which are among the groups that in recent months have spent upwards of $30 million lobbying Congress to pass the Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan bill that would grant the governing body antitrust protection and shield it from litigation around issues like eligibility, NIL and the transfer portal.

Kiffin’s gambit this offseason has certainly caused a public relations headache for the NCAA and the conference, most observers agree, but some predict the saga could end up being a catalyst for necessary change in college sports.

“It’s hard to know what the rules are in college football specifically anymore. It feels like they’re being created more by judges than by the NCAA or conferences,” said Kevin Paule, another sports business attorney. “This definitely helps the supporters of the Senate bill. They can more easily make the argument ‘look at this, we are trying to do something about this and the bill would either make these situations disappear or be far less likely in the future.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) is reportedly investigating the Los Angeles Clippers over a scheme to funnel money through sponsors and other team business partners to star player Kawhi Leonard to circumvent the NBA salary cap. The probe, first reported by The New York Times, comes after the league handed down sanctions against the team, docking it five draft picks and banning billionaire owner Steve Ballmer from team activities for a year. It was unclear as of last week whether Ballmer or Leonard specifically are potential targets of the DOJ’s criminal probe.

President Trump said in a Truth Social post his address at the Republican midterm convention on Wednesday “beat” the NFL on opening night in terms of audience. It was a claim that came with no reference to specific viewership or social media engagement numbers. The president’s address was carried in full by only a few cable channels, while national broadcast network NBC has not publicized ratings from the Seahawks vs. Patriots game. A typical audience for an NFL game in primetime comes in the tens of millions in terms of average viewership.

Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R) published a new ad last week showing him swinging a baseball bat in a batting cage while listing off his policy prerogatives. The former 2024 GOP presidential candidate and Trump ally was hit with some jeers on social media and criticism from hitting coaches over his technique at the plate.

Jocks on the Hill: Rep. Morgan McGarvey (D-Ky.)

Rep. Morgan McGarvey, the only Democrat in the Kentucky congressional delegation, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“Man … my favorite playing was baseball. I only played through Little League, but I enjoyed it.”

“I root for teams that when I was a kid weren’t rivals and are now rivals. So when I was growing up the [St. Louis] Cardinals had their Triple A affiliate in Louisville. So we had the Red Birds, we went to those games all the times and saw all the Cardinals come up. But Cincinnati is about an hour and a half from Louisville. So I would go with my grandfather up to see the Reds. It was the first pro team I ever got to see. Plus, anyone who grew up in South roots for the Braves because they were on TV.”

Is there an athlete you really admired growing up?

“You know, I really liked Greg Maddux. He was really dominant. And I liked the fact he was such a student of the game and he looked like your English professor and then would get up there and dominate you.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“Everybody in Kentucky roots against Duke.”

The legendary NHL coach and ESPN hockey commentator Barry Melrose died last week after a battle with Parkinson’s disease. One of the outlet’s lead hockey reporters, Greg Wyshynski, penned a touching tribute to Melrose, writing that for many fans, he simply “was hockey.”

The investigative news outlet ProPublica published a deeply reported piece examining the Dominican Republic’s production of more MLB players than any country outside the U.S. It found an essentially unregulated industry that uses “enormous sums promised to poor families” and reported that moneylenders exploit players and their families “by offering loans at exorbitant interest rates” and then finding ways “to scam them.”

Tennis at 3 in the morning? Really? The Wall Street Journal sports columnist Jason Gay takes the U.S. Open to task in this new piece , writing it’s another example of an instance where “this glorious sport can’t get out of its own way.”

articles.title: DSA-backed candidates are winning primaries and their vision for America is very different
articles.summary: Democratic Socialists of America launched its "Workers Deserve More" program calling for public ownership, a 32-hour workweek and universal healthcare.
articles.body: The Democratic Socialists of America is seeking to reshape some of the most basic features of the U.S. economy — from who owns major corporations to how long Americans work and whether families pay for healthcare, college and housing. The agenda is drawing renewed scrutiny after DSA-backed candidates gained ground in the 2026 midterm primaries and progressive socialism became a central Republican target at the GOP's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas. Below are some of the biggest economic proposals in the platform. Public ownership of major corporations and industries DSA calls for public ownership of major corporations and essential industries, arguing public ownership would give Americans greater democratic control over the economy. Adam Lehodey, a policy expert at the Manhattan Institute, said nationalizing major corporations would cost billions of dollars and shift accountability from customers to government officials. 'WASTEFUL DISTRACTION': EXPERTS SLAM MAMDANI'S TAXPAYER-FUNDED STORES He argued nationalized industries have historically suffered from waste, corruption and lower productivity, adding that reducing regulations would be a better way to encourage competition. A 32-hour workweek with full pay DSA also wants to establish a 32-hour workweek without reducing workers' pay or benefits, effectively giving full-time employees an additional day away from work while preserving their compensation. The proposal is paired with a living minimum wage, paid family leave and stronger protections for workers to form unions and strike. TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE The agenda does not explain how a shorter workweek would be implemented across industries or how businesses would be expected to absorb the additional labor costs. Lehodey said a 32-hour workweek without higher productivity could increase labor costs and reduce economic output. Universal healthcare, housing and education Among DSA's biggest proposals are universal healthcare, publicly owned social housing, free public education through college and cancellation of all student debt. Together, the proposals would shift a much larger share of healthcare, housing and education costs from individuals to the federal government. A Cato Institute analysis estimated that a Medicare-for-All-style healthcare system alone could increase federal spending by between $40 trillion and $75 trillion over a decade, though the estimate is not specific to DSA's proposal. Higher taxes on wealthy Americans and corporations DSA says wealthy Americans and large corporations should shoulder more of the cost of its vision. The platform calls for "aggressive wealth taxes" on the richest individuals and corporations, with the proceeds directed toward public goods and infrastructure. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lehodey questioned whether wealthy taxpayers alone could finance the agenda, arguing broader taxpayers would likely bear some of the cost. DSA's platform does not estimate the total cost of its agenda or how much revenue its proposed tax increases would generate.

articles.title: Unearthed clip shows Talarico calling parents 'abusive' for denying children's gender identity
articles.summary: James Talarico, the Democratic Texas Senate candidate, once called parents' refusal to acknowledge a child's gender identity "abusive" behavior.
articles.body: James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once described parents who refused to acknowledge their children’s gender identity as potentially engaging in "abusive" behavior. "I think there are some folks that would think that if you deny your child's gender identity, that's incredibly harmful. And whether or not we label it with the term abuse, it's abusive for sure," Talarico said while speaking at a committee hearing in the Texas Legislature in 2019. Talarico’s resurfaced comments add to a growing pile of past remarks that cut against his efforts to paint himself as a moderate on issues like gender, policing and border security as he attempts to win over Texas, a historically Republican-leaning state. TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS In the clip, Talarico had been speaking about HB 1910. The legislation aimed to ensure that parents who refused to affirm their child’s gender identity would not be considered guilty of child abuse in cases deciding custody. "In determining whether to appoint a party as a sole or joint managing conservator of a child, the court may not consider evidence regarding whether the party demonstrates a history or pattern of acknowledging or declining to acknowledge the child’s gender identity or expression," its text read. Talarico opposed the bill, arguing that he would not rule out an overlap: that, in some cases, the lack of acknowledgment could border on abuse. "My concern is ruling it out as not being abuse, I think, is dangerous and could certainly harm some of our most vulnerable kids in the state." TALARICO CAMPAIGNS WITH SURGEON WHO OPERATED ON TRANSGENDER MINORS: ‘WOLF IN SHEEP’S CLOTHING’ "Some of us I think really do consider this abusive behavior… an unwillingness to identify, acknowledge a child's gender identity. We consider that abusive to the child, abusive and destructive," Talarico said. At least one Republican slammed Talarico's stance. "Only perverts and pedophiles think about what is in little kids' pants as much as James Talafreako. He is a truly sick individual for dedicating his life to pushing sex changes on other people's kids," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Although that version of the bill died in committee, a later, stronger version of it eventually passed out of the Texas House in May 2025 and became law. EXCLUSIVE: HOUSE COMMITTEE PROBES CHICAGO PUBLIC SCHOOLS OVER HIDING 'GENDER AFFIRMATION' FROM PARENTS Talarico also opposed that version — one of 59 nay votes on the matter. Notably, Talarico also voted in favor of an amendment to sunset the law in 2030 and in support of a separate amendment clarifying that, in the words of its author, "rejecting a child's gender identity or sexual orientation is abuse" and "should be treated as such under Texas law." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When asked about the bill and his statements in committee, the Talarico campaign said he supported and respected parental decisions about their children. "James believes parents have the most important say in decisions about their children, which is why he sponsored a bill to protect parental rights and ensure parents are responsible for the upbringing of their own kids. While James has fought for Texas parents and families, Ken Paxton has endangered them by allowing pedophiles back on our streets," JT Ennis, a spokesperson for the Talarico campaign, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Our media can’t even tell who is sympathetic anymore
articles.summary: Are we so far out of touch that now we offer political strategists, identity thieves, academic fraudsters and even actual robbers and murderers as the sympathetic face of the cause?
articles.body:
Of all the factors contributing to the media’s crisis of credibility, few are as harmful as its ideological monoculture.

When the overwhelming majority of those in a small but influential industry believe the same things, talk about the same things, attend the same schools, go to the same parties, watch the same shows, read the same books, and vote for the same party, it is easy for them to adopt a narrow worldview, losing all sense of self-awareness along the way.

Consider the New Yorker , which last week published a feature that cast as an object of deep sympathy a noncitizen who specializes in U.S. election engineering. Daysi Gonzalez came from El Salvador on a tourist visa but stayed after her home country qualified for temporary protected status following a series of earthquakes in 2001. She may soon have to leave because that not-so-temporary program finally expired last week.

“Unlike most immigrants in America, Gonzalez has a job that puts her in rooms with powerful people,” the profile reads. “As a partner at the consulting firm Solidarity Strategies, she tries to help Democrats win some of the most consequential races in the country. … Her biggest client this cycle is the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, which has paid her firm more than a hundred and eighty thousand dollars this year.”

This raises the question: Has our insularity so destroyed our sense of what makes a figure sympathetic that we now offer as the face of the cause a foreign national who is paid (and paid very handsomely) to meddle in U.S. elections?

Of the twenty-five years Gonzalez has spent here as a noncitizen, nearly ten have gone to political consulting. She has worked on issue advocacy, ballot referenda and Democratic campaigns through nearly half a dozen election cycles, including this one. She explored a few paths to citizenship, including an H-1B lottery bid, and declined to pursue others, including marriage. She found no immediate way forward. Her boss, political consultant Chuck Rocha, is frustrated that his attempts to skirt immigration law by pulling strings have failed.

The New Yorker answers all this with a naked appeal for pity. It treats as a minor tragedy the prospect that Gonzalez — a non-voting noncitizen whose bread and butter is U.S. election engineering — may soon have to return to her home country.

The New Yorker may characterize it as a tragedy, but not everyone thinks it a tragedy when rich foreigners cannot tinker in U.S. elections.

Even so, Gonzalez’s story hardly holds a candle to the New York Times ‘ even more preposterous feature last week, bemoaning that artificial intelligence has made it harder for Kenyans to make money by helping foreign students cheat in school.

The Times story follows Teresios Bundi, who once made a fine living writing papers for American academic cheaters. “He sometimes considered the ethics of helping students cheat, but decided it was ultimately their choice,” the story reads. “He said he saw himself as a tutor and was proud that a young Kenyan was thriving unnoticed inside Western academia. … Essay writers drove new Subarus, carried the latest smartphones and booked exclusive tables at clubs.” Then AI arrived, “and the good times ended. … Kenya’s experience shows how the technology is already dismantling some lower rungs of the global labor market,” the Times warns.

If the aim is to raise awareness about AI job loss, surely the Times could have found someone more sympathetic than the middlemen in a global academic fraud scheme. And by the way, this A.I. profile was in addition to a separate Times article last week that complained that a raid on an illegal gambling and drug ring in Tennessee, run by a twice-deported Honduran felon, led to multiple other deportations and put enough fear into the local illegal immigrant community that people are afraid to go out and party.

And if you think that’s bad, wait until you see the Times profile of Romeo Perez-Bravo , a thrice-deported illegal immigrant from Guatemala with convictions for domestic violence and forgery who stole an American’s identity. Perez ruined his victim’s credit and caused him to pay thousands in wrongful fees and garnished wages when the IRS came after the wrong man. The American victim was even sued for wrongful death after Perez was involved in a fatal car accident — a crash apparently unrelated to Perez’s six drunk-driving convictions.

Yet this is the headline the Times chose for the story: “Two Men. One Identity. They Both Paid the Price.” Perez was just sentenced to seven years in federal prison last month — perhaps we’ll get another sympathetic Times profile when he finishes his sentence and is deported for a fourth time in 2033.

Nor should we forget when the New Yorker published this whopper of a blurb : “Orville Etoria, a Jamaican national who’d lived in New York for nearly 50 years, was shackled and put on an ICE flight to Eswatini. ‘It helped me imagine how the slaves might have felt, going to another land in shackles and chains,’ he said.”

Etoria had been convicted of multiple serious felonies, including armed robbery and murder. Of the nearly 50 years he spent in New York, 25 were in state prison on a murder sentence. He did part of that time at Sing Sing, the maximum-security prison where he earned a bachelor’s degree. He had already served about three years for other offenses in the 1980s.

Etoria was issued a final order of removal in 2009, but despite his lengthy criminal history of victimizing Americans, he somehow managed to stay in the U.S. for another decade.

Are we so far out of touch that now we offer political strategists, identity thieves, academic fraudsters and even actual robbers and murderers as the sympathetic face of the cause? Are we all out of orphans and widows? Do you profile writers even hear yourselves?

The late film critic Pauline Kael identified and articulated this flavor of insularity as early as 1972, in remarks that would be badly misremembered : “I live in a rather special world,” she said. “I only know one person who voted for Nixon. Where they are I don’t know. They’re outside my ken. But sometimes when I’m in a theater I can feel them.”

Nixon had won that year in a landslide, with 60 percent of the popular vote and 520 electoral votes.

For Kael, to know only one person who helped make those numbers possible was merely embarrassing. The problem now is that her narrow outlook has become a feature, not a bug, of the modern news industry.

For an industry to be this far removed from the concerns and ideas of ordinary readers is more than embarrassing. It is untenable.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Congress faces frenzy of AI fears: ‘The monster is loose’
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Calls for Congress to regulate AI ▪ Trump to remove tariffs on Irish whiskey ▪ Trump wants to keep a hand in Iran oil ▪ House GOP bets on Trump Congress returns this week to an eruption of fears about the future of artificial intelligence (AI) spurred by warnings from within the industry that…
articles.body:
▪ Trump to remove tariffs on Irish whiskey

▪ Trump wants to keep a hand in Iran oil

Congress returns this week to an eruption of fears about the future of artificial intelligence (AI) spurred by warnings from within the industry that it could take over the internet or even destroy humanity in the near future.

Congressional leaders already appear torn between President Trump ‘s position that any significant regulations risk throttling progress and ceding the AI race to China, and urgent calls for guardrails to ensure the technology does not harm humanity.

The House has just one week left on its calendar before November’s midterm elections. Axios reported that members are urging Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to cancel the recess until Congress can pass AI safeguards.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said Sunday he supports immediate congressional action .

“We certainly need to begin to act urgently to address the challenges that exist,” Jeffries told host George Stephanopoulos on ABC’s “This Week.”

Jeffries noted “action” on AI will be a “high priority” during his caucus’s closed-door meeting on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Johnson urged people not to panic and said lawmakers do not want to smother innovation.

“If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American. So, we’ve got to have balance. We’ve got to have steady hands at the wheel ,” Johnson told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Sunday.

Trump sounded a similar note while speaking to reporters at his golf club in Doonbeg, Ireland, on Sunday, saying that guardrails can be installed, but he doesn’t want to lose to China in the process.

“Well, I say this, we’re leading China on AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world and frankly I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins,” he said.

The debate comes after AI researchers and leaders took to social media to sound the alarm on the pace of AI growth.

Jacob Coxon , a former Anthropic researcher who also worked for OpenAI, warned on Tuesday that AI could soon destroy humanity.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” he wrote on social platform X .

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he added.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei echoed the warning on Saturday in a blog post titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.” He did not argue for a full stop, but instead that companies should take time to build safeguards.

“I believe that if slowing down bought us even an extra year or two before models reach critical levels of capability, and we used that time to advance alignment, we could greatly reduce the risk that something goes seriously wrong,” he wrote.

He specifically called for “regulation that targets all US frontier AI companies, as that covers even those who are unwilling to cooperate voluntarily.”

Elon Musk of xAI and SpaceX on Saturday said, “Dario is right,” in a post on X. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, also took to social media in support of Amodei’s plea.

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) on Sunday told CNN’s Tapper that AI is more powerful than past technologies and therefore requires different standards for regulation.

“This is more akin to Dr. Frankenstein telling us, ‘The monster is loose. Help me stop the monster,’” he said during his “State of the Union” appearance. “Previous tech could not make a decision to kill us, right? When we turned on the internet, it did not have autonomy, right? ”

However, David Sacks , a tech investor who stepped down as the White House AI czar earlier this year, said leading AI companies should take the initiative themselves.

“If the unreleased models are scary enough that you think you should slow down, I support your decision to be responsible. But stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission,” he wrote, lising other issues with Amodei’s post.

“Most of all, stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyberattack,” he added.

Rep. Mike Flood (R-Neb.) during an interview on NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday” said suggested a methodical approach to the issue.

“This shouldn’t be ready, shoot, aim or shoot, ready, aim. It should be, ‘Let’s find out what exactly we’re talking about here.’ If it is as dire as they say, obviously, it warrants action, but we need to get the facts before we rush in and say, ‘We’ve got a solution,’” the Nebraska Republican told host Chris Stirewalt on Sunday.

Given the president’s wariness of regulations and general partisan gridlock, those calling for urgent action face an uphill battle during this session. But the debate in the coming weeks could offer clues about where Democrats would steer AI regulations if they win back power in November.

Former President Obama sent a message to Jeffries at a private fundraiser on Thursday: “Once you are speaker, I would strongly urge that the Democrats put together a framework for a very public conversation,” he said, The New York Times reports .

And he said candidates vying for president in 2028 make artificial intelligence part of their central agenda.

▪ The Hill : Debate, confusion explodes over AI ‘doomsday’ warnings.

▪ The Hill : Johnson on AI regulation: ‘We don’t need everybody to panic right now.’

▪ The Hill : Jeffries says Congress should ‘act urgently’ on AI safeguards.

Trump will remove tariffs on Irish whiskey , he announced Sunday while visiting Ireland for the Amgen Irish Open golf tournament. The president said he was swayed by Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Irish golfer Shane Lowry to lift the tax, in a decision Trump referred to as“a favor.”

Asked about potentially impeaching the president , Jeffries told ABC’s George Stephanopoulos that should Democrats regain control of the House, he and his colleagues “haven’t ruled anything out.”

Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command , said he is “not concerned at all” about the U.S.’s munitions inventories amid reports that the Pentagon has depleted its stockpiles to fight Iran.

President Trump attends the Irish Open golf tournament at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, Ireland, on Sept. 13, 2026.

HOT BUTTON : In a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, Ireland, on Saturday, Trump spoke positively about the unification of the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, which is currently part of the United Kingdom.

“I’d love to see it unified,” the president said. “I think that’d be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.”

It is atypical for an American president to weigh so directly into one of Europe’s most contentious geopolitical debates. Trump’s decision to break that norm spurred some angry responses, even from his allies across the pond.

Leader of the Reform U.K. party Nigel Farage took to social media to disagree with Trump, writing that the “people of Northern Ireland neither want a referendum, nor unification.”

Gavin Robinson , who heads the U.K.’s Democratic Unionist Party and represents Northern Ireland in Parliament,” wrote on X: “Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.”

But the president on Sunday doubled down after arriving at Doonbeg’s first tee box.

“I’ve always loved the people of Ireland and it just seems to me that you have Northern Ireland and you have Ireland, and it would seem to me that one of the naturals of all time is put them together … many people agree,” he said.

▪ The Associated Press : Trump’s backing for a united Ireland has reignited a divisive political issue. Here’s what to know.

PACKED AGENDA: The House and Senate are back. The legislative calendar has been cut short following the House’s decision to depart Washington on Thursday for recess and return after the November midterm elections, but there is still a lot to do.

The Senate is set to continue talks on a budget resolution to move closer toward unlocking a third reconciliation bill. The Senate Agriculture Committee will vote on a farm bill that failed to advance last month due to Republican absences and Democratic opposition. The Senate will also hold a procedural vote on the Clarity Act, although it is not expected to have Democrats’ support due to a lack of an ethics provision.

Meanwhile, the House will consider a Russia sanctions bill that has passed the Senate. It will also put the Ratepayer Protection Act on the floor to mitigate the impact of data center costs on household electric bills. It is expected to garner bipartisan support.

▪ The Hill : This week on The Hill: Congress returns to a packed agenda.

LONG HAUL: Trump on Sunday suggested that the U.S. might remain in Iran and “keep the oil,” comparing the potential idea to the recent deal made with Venezuela.

While in Doonbeg, the president reiterated his feelings that the Iran war will finish by the midterms, also stating that Iranian leadership “wants to make a deal so badly, and is calling constantly.”

“We’ll ultimately get out unless we decide to stay and keep the oil, like Venezuela,” the president added.

Late last month, the Trump administration struck a deal with the South American country’s second-largest privately-owned oil producer, North American Blue Energy Partners, giving the U.S. shared control over 17 oil fields in Venezuela.

Iran and it’s proxies have expanded the war in recent days, with tensions flaring in the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthis in Yemen seizing a strategic port along a key Red Sea shipping lane.

The average price of gas in the U.S. hit $4.31 on Sunday, over $1.10 higher than last year’s average, according to data from AAA.

▪ The Hill : President Trump suggests US may stay and keep Iran oil like Venezuela deal.

PUMPING THE BRAKES: GOP concern is growing over the president’s proposed $5,000 dividends, which he announced Wednesday. The president said the money would be dispersed to all U.S. adults should the GOP maintain its control over Congress come November.

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) shifted his stance on the dividends, after posting a supportive message on X last week.

“I’m going to bring in all the information, and then make a decision,” Marshall, who is up for reelection, said while debating Democratic opponent Adam Hamilton .

“But look, this is not the first time I’ve disagreed with President Trump, and it probably won’t be the last.”

Marshall isn’t the only GOP lawmaker wary of the proposal, which would cost more than $1 trillion.

“First thing, I think we need to see the proposal, but the priority, in my opinion right now, should be funding our troops and replenishing our munitions before we do anything,” Flood said Sunday during his appearance on “The Hill Sunday.”

A number of GOP deficit hawks were quick to blast Trump’s idea last week.

▪ The Hill : Trump says $5K dividend checks to Americans will ‘happen 100 percent.’

The president holds executive time and policy meetings throughout the day starting at 8:30 a.m. EDT.

House Majority Leader Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.) speaks at the Republican convention on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas, Texas.

BETTING ON TRUMP: Republican leaders in the House are betting that Trump will help the party defy expectations in the midterm elections and maintain control over the lower chamber.

Some political experts are wondering if that’s the right strategy as the president is mired in consistently low approval ratings amid an unpopular war in Iran and high prices at home.

But the GOP’s message was clear at the midterm convention in Texas last week, with House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) saying Trump’s “America First agenda is at stake” in the November elections.

“This was designed to activate [the] base, but you can’t help but also wonder if it just further defines MAGA to swing voters — Independents in particular — as a weird, cultish movement, because there was a heavy vibe of that,” Rob Stutzman , a California-based Republican consultant, told The Hill’s Mike Lillis .

A recent poll from Reuters/Ipsos found Trump’s approval rating at the lowest point between his two presidencies. Voters also favored Democrats to take control of the House by an 11-point margin in a Quinnipiac University survey published late last week.

While GOP House leadership is doubling down on the president’s base, some Republican incumbents and candidates are choosing to keep Trump at arm’s length, as they figure out how the president factors into their own political calculus, The Hill’s Julia Manchester reported over the weekend .

A child plays on top of a deteriorated classic American car in Regla, Cuba, on Sept. 7, 2026.

CUBAN CONCERNS: Leading Cuban political activists are supportive of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign against their island nation’s communist regime.

They just want a bigger voice in the process.

That’s what two leading voices in the Cuban opposition and democratic movement told The Hill’s Laura Kelly . José Daniel Ferrer , a Cuban political activist exiled in Miami, and Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara , who was released from Cuban prison in July after direct U.S. intervention, were presented the National Endowment for Democracy’s freedom of speech award last week.

“This is perhaps the best chance that something will occur,” Ferrer told The Hill, referring to the Trump administration’s moves against the Cuban regime.

Trump — at least publicly — has not spoken nearly as often in recent months about Cuba as he did after the U.S. toppled Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in early January. The president at the time said Cuba, which shares deep ties with Venezuela, could be next .

But Kelly reports that negotiations over a possible exit of Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel have stalled, and what’s next is unclear.

Still, Trump earlier this month posted a map with an American flag emblazoned over most of North America and some Caribbean islands — including Cuba.

Trump’s coastal grab should alarm all Americans , Christine Todd Whittman writes in The Hill.

Biden and Trump called it a genocide and then turned away , Nicholas Kristof writes in The New York Times.

Turning Point USA Founder Charlie Kirk speaks during a campaign rally, Oct. 24, 2024, in Las Vegas.

And finally … A statue of Charlie Kirk outside of Turning Point USA’s (TPUSA) headquarters was vandalized.

TPUSA shared images of the statue and an accompanying sign, which both appear to be defaced with red spray paint. The conservative media organization announced that they would “restore the statue and replace the signs,” adding that they planned to identify those involved.

“But vandalism like this is not funny, it’s diabolical. The incident happened in the middle of the night because evil never sleeps,” the organization wrote in a social media post .

“ Beyond spray painting on the neck and face, they made the intentional decision to cross out the name of Jesus on a nearby sign,” TPUSA added.

articles.title: Deadly silence: The world can’t afford to ignore climate change much longer
articles.summary: Sixty years of inaction in Washington have not made climate change go away. Hushing won’t either. In the meantime, the American people, present and future, are paying an increasingly intolerable price.
articles.body:
Our government could do something about climate change, but it refuses. In fact, most elected leaders and political candidates don’t even talk about it.

As the fossil-fuel industry increasingly allied itself with Republicans to block climate action over the decades, Democrats became the party more willing to address it. But now, even many Democrats have gone quiet. As the November midterms approach, think tanks and consultants are advising them to avoid the topic global warming because “it is not a priority for voters.”

The silence is called “ climate hushing, ” the strategic choice to avoid talking about global warming to avoid political backlash, polarization or economic anxiety. In other words, our elected leaders should avoid mentioning the huge elephant in the room, even as it gets more dangerous.

Hardly an evening newscast goes by today without reports of major weather disasters and millions of Americans under threat of fire, flood, killer heat or other calamity. Community after community is turned to ash by wildfires, blown into rubble by tornadoes or washed away in flash floods.

Last year, major weather disasters struck the U.S. every 10 days , on average. Billion-dollar disasters have occurred every 16 days on average over the last decade, compared to every 82 days in the 1980s. And those figures count only the most destructive disasters — thousands of smaller floods, fires, storms and other extreme-weather events never make the billion-dollar list, although they can be catastrophic to the families and communities they strike.

The numbers don’t convey the profound human costs: injury and death, lost homes, emotional trauma, economic calamity, lifetime treasures lost forever. There are no true climate havens . Risks differ from place to place, but no region is immune.

The numbers also don’t convey the distress and anxiety children and young adults feel as they face a future of even worse global warming and climate disasters.

This is the irony of climate hushing: Consultants advise candidates to talk about affordability instead of climate change, when climate change is increasingly an affordability issue. It reduces property values, damages public health, raises taxes, increases the federal deficit, and more.

A year-old Brookings study , based on only a few types of climate-related impacts, found that U.S. households pay as much as $900 per year on average because of climate change, and more than $1,300 in hardest-hit counties.

The average premium for homeowners insurance increased 8.7 percent faster than inflation from 2018 through 2022. Homeowners in the highest-risk ZIP codes paid 82 percent more on average than those in the lowest-risk areas — and were substantially more likely to lose their coverage altogether.

On the other hand, policies that reduce fossil-fuel pollution can save significant money. As much as 80 percent of America’s air pollution comes from fossil fuels. A 2021 synthesis of scientific research estimated the pollution and climate-related health impacts impose more than $820 billion a year in health damages in the U.S., including premature deaths, illness, hospitalizations and lost wages.

A study late last year by the Center for American Progress reported that “climate-accelerated shocks are contributing to some of the largest food price increases American families have faced in recent years.” Beef is an example — as prolonged drought reduced cattle herds, the Department of Agriculture projected a 12 percent increase in beef and veal prices.

Yet through 11 presidents and 31 Congresses over the last 60 years, our national government has failed to act in a manner commensurate with the scale and duration of the crisis. That failure is not only a dereliction of duty; it’s increasingly recognized as a crime against humanity , present and future.

The American people don’t need silence from political leaders who fear retribution. They need facts. Political consultants ask what voters want politicians to talk about. Leaders must also ask what voters need to know. Polls seem to contradict the advice that climate-hushing is a good campaign strategy. Six in 10 voters prefer candidates who support climate action, while only 14 percent oppose it. More than four in 10 voters want politicians to talk about it more.

We need leaders today, like those of the past, who inspire the country to take on big challenges. Franklin Roosevelt called on America to be the “great arsenal of democracy” in World War II. John F. Kennedy wanted America to put the first man on the moon. He said it would be difficult, but it would “ organize and measure the best of our energies and skills. ” That is the case with climate action, too.

To be fair, not all leaders are hushing. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) has made the case for climate action in 308 speeches on the Senate floor . But our leaders need to make the case directly to the people and inspire them with the benefits of acting.

Sixty years of inaction in Washington have not made climate change go away. Hushing won’t either. In the meantime, the American people, present and future, are paying an increasingly intolerable price.

William S. Becker is a former regional director at the U.S. Department of Energy and author of several books on climate change and national disaster policies.

articles.title: Schumer calls for classified briefing on danger posed by AI
articles.summary: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Monday called on the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to all senators on the dangers posed by AI after a researcher for Anthropic warned that companies chasing artificial superintelligence are “gambling with our lives.” “The American people deserve better from their government at such a consequential…
articles.body:
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) on Monday called on the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to all senators on the dangers posed by AI after a researcher for Anthropic warned that companies chasing artificial superintelligence are “gambling with our lives.”

“The American people deserve better from their government at such a consequential moment. I have long argued that we must keep the U.S. as the global leader in AI innovation and security,” Schumer said in a statement.

He added, “But that innovation must be coupled with serious guardrails that earn the trust of the American public.”

“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have — and the Trump administration is looking the other way,” the senator continued. “Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must.”

Schumer said officials in President Trump’s administration need to answer questions about three areas of concern related to AI.

First, he wants the administration to provide senators with a full accounting of its new framework for testing the most powerful frontier AI model. Next, the New York Democrat pressed the administration to detail what it’s doing to prevent AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment from flowing to China.

Finally, he asked the White House to explain its plans to defend the U.S. from increasingly sophisticated AI-enabled cyberattacks.

The request comes as others on Capitol Hill have called for briefings or more guardrails on the emerging technology. Trump and GOP leaders, however, have pushed back on the growing AI fears .

articles.title: DC’s attorney general wants to be the new national speech czar
articles.summary: Consumer protection laws are supposed to make sure products work as advertised, not that companies toe the D.C. government’s line on climate change.
articles.body:
The attorney general of Washington, D.C., a person few Americans have ever heard of, wants to be the nation’s top speech cop. Progressive municipalities across the country are suing energy companies over their speech about climate change.

The District’s attorney general, Brian Schwalb, has brought a climate speech lawsuit with scary knock-on effects for the entire country.

Schwalb holds a high leverage position, with disproportionate power to rig political debates for the left. Foundations, think tanks, advocacy groups, and trade associations line every block of the nation’s capital. They brief reporters, organize events, lobby decisionmakers, and incubate new policy ideas.

Schwalb is threatening all of that First Amendment activity by weaponizing consumer protection laws against targets he dislikes. And given Washington’s far-left political character, the threat falls only one way.

Climate lawsuits accuse energy producers of duping consumers by concealing ties between energy products and global warming. The evidence? Newspaper ads and policy statements from industry trade groups — their ordinary political advocacy, as a federal judge recently admitted from the bench.

Consider the breathtaking reach of Schwalb’s theory. Any statement posted on any website, anywhere in the world, at any time, can expose the speaker to consumer protection liability in the District of Columbia — even without proof that a single consumer within its borders ever saw the statement, much less relied on it when pumping gas.

On this theory, merely posting a statement online supplies the jurisdictional hook to haul a defendant into D.C. Superior Court. Every company, think tank, advocacy group and individual with a website that crosses green orthodoxy could face years of litigation in Schwalb’s home court.

The District’s “front group” theory sweeps even wider. Schwalb alleges the companies laundered deceptive messages through third parties, such as the American Petroleum Institute. Where does that end? If a retired energy executive who owns company stock donates to a think tank skeptical of climate alarmism, is he running a front group? What about the newspaper that accepts the industry’s advertisement or publishes its op-ed? On Schwalb’s logic, they are all in on the scheme.

And climate is only the opening act. California’s attorney general has already sued ExxonMobil over its statements about plastics recycling. In fact, any Washington think tank that takes the industry’s side in a fight over plastics, gas stoves, or processed food could find its policy papers recast as a form of consumer fraud.

Remember, consumer protection law requires no intent to deceive. In 1994, Al Gore cast the tie-breaking Senate vote for the ethanol mandate , when ethanol was hailed as an environmental winner. By 2010, he was admitting his mistake and confessing he backed it partly out of fondness for Tennessee corn farmers. So, under Schwalb’s theory, was the Gore campaign a front group for corn growers committing consumer fraud?

Apart from its menacing implications for the First Amendment, the District’s legal claims are weak on their own terms. Some the contested claims are true statements. Many energy companies produce low-emission fuels and lubricants. Exxon produces motor oil which lowers emissions by improving engine performance. Shell sells gas products that cut emissions by stopping buildup of engine gunk.

Schwalb does not claim that these statements are false. He cannot, because they aren’t. Instead, he says marketing those products without mentioning climate change amounts to tricking the customer.

I am not aware of any other consumer protection case in which a company got in trouble for telling the truth about its products.

Many of the supposedly actionable statements Schwalb cites are mere corporate platitudes. The complaint faults Shell, for example, for its stated commitment to balancing “economic progress with environmental care and social responsibility.” BP is faulted for an advertisement professing a commitment “to make our energy cleaner and better.” But those statements aren’t deceptive — they are just banal.

Perhaps most importantly, Schwalb will attack energy companies no matter what they do about climate change. Say too little, and the company is staging a corporate coverup (this is the “Exxon Knew” campaign). Say too much, and the company is accused of “greenwashing” its products. There is no satisfying the climate plaintiffs. Their satisfaction is in destroying energy companies, not in serious enforcement of consumer protection statutes.

The consumer protection laws police hidden fees, defective products and false advertisements that manipulate purchases. The nub of the law in this area is the question, “Does the product work as advertised to the customer?” No one disputes that energy products work as advertised. In fact, the District government itself still burns fossil fuels to heat its buildings, power its police cars and school buses, and fly its officials to various locations on city business. Does that sound like a defective product?

Ultimately the climate-consumer protection claims rest on the false premise that consumers are stupid or have been deluded about climate change all along. But climate policy has been a fixture of political debate for decades. Businesses, advocacy groups, and voters can reasonably debate how to protect our communities without destroying them. Those disagreements are not deceptive or unlawful.

Washington D.C.’s climate lawsuit is menacing to the future of free speech in our country. Extremists are emerging from Democratic primaries lately. It is easy to imagine the Democratic Socialists of America electing their first attorney general in Washington, D.C. Schwalb has left a very dangerous precedent for that person to exploit in silencing all political opposition.

Todd J. Zywicki is George Mason University Foundation Professor of Law at George Mason University Antonin Scalia Law School and Co-Director of Institute for Consumer Financial Choice.
